AP&E Studio — Recording Brief

Date: 2026-10-01Version 2.0 — every distinct recording described individuallyProduction contact: AP&E StudioAudience: recording engineer

A · About this brief

What this is for

AP&E Studio is an interactive pro-audio training app. Learners work through labs — microphones, speech, EQ, dynamics, mixing, mastering, live sound, cables, acoustics, post-production — and hear the sound change while they move the controls on screen: they rotate a mic and hear the rear go quiet and dull, drag a distance fader and hear the room take over, flip polarity and hear a snare thin out. Most of those pages are silent today, or play a synthesized stand-in. Your recordings replace them. Accuracy matters because learners copy real technique from what they hear: a mislabelled pattern, a normalized fixed-gain set or a processed “dry” vocal would teach the wrong thing.

The 89 item cards describe 523 distinct recordings (495 of them in active, non-reuse items). Priority of the 89 items: P1 22 · P2 43 · P3 24. Of these, 8 are reuse-only cards (no new files: they point at files recorded under another item), 1 is optional and 2 are on hold (19 held files, not counted above). The 593 files are 464 new recordings plus 129 edited or derived files (loudness-matched copies, loop cuts, deconvolved impulse responses, stereo balances and as-authored copies).

P1 — do first: MIX-01, MST-01, MPR-01, MPR-02, MPR-03, MPR-04a, MPR-04b, MPR-05a, MPR-05b, MPR-06, SPC-01, SPC-02, SPC-04, DES-01, EQ-01a, EQ-01b, EQ-01c, EQ-01d, EQ-01e, FX-01, SS-01.

How to use this document

  1. Read B (spec), C (scripts) and F (safety) once before booking anything. They apply to every item.
  2. Plan from E (sessions). Each session lists the gear, room, people, time and an ordered shot list that keeps resets to a minimum.
  3. Work from the item cards in D. Each card opens with what the learner does on that lab page, then contains one section per distinct recording (for example MIX-01.3), each with its own context, teaching goal, method, tips, specs, file list with tick boxes and quality check. Recordings share a section only when they are identical in method, context and teaching. P1 cards and their recordings open by default; the contents list can expand each lab's recording IDs.
  4. “Reuse — no new recording” rows and cards point at a file you already made for another item. Never record those twice.
  5. Filter with the search box, the priority boxes and the session menu (needs JavaScript; with it off, everything is simply shown). Ticks are saved only in your browser.
  6. Before delivery, run G (global + per-file QC) and fill the sidecars and manifest.
  7. Questions, substitutions (e.g. the alto flute for FND-01) or anything you cannot capture honestly: write it in the manifest notes. Never fake a sound to fill a row.

B · Global technical spec

Applies to every item unless its card says otherwise.

FormatWAV PCM, 48 kHz / 24-bit. Mono unless the item says stereo. Never 44.1 kHz or 16-bit, except the deliberate PROD-01 “as authored” files.
EditingEdit only: trim, with 5–10 ms fades at zero crossings. For sustained loops (organ, hum, noise beds) a loop crossfade of ≤ 50 ms is allowed; for 2.000 s Ear Training excerpts ≤ 20 ms.
ProcessingNONE: no EQ, compression, limiting, reverb, noise reduction, de-essing, pitch correction or normalizing. Exceptions are named in the item: the produced mixes (MIX-03, MST-01 b, MST-02), deconvolved impulse responses, the M/S decode, the EAR-06 polarity flip, the PROD-01 sample-rate conversion and the PROD-02 edit click.
PeaksSample peak ≤ −6 dBFS, never clipped. One-shots and plosive takes may peak at −3 dBFS. Mastered references: as specified (see Safety).
Sustained levelSustained or looping sources: RMS about −20 dBFS (where an item says −18 dBFS RMS, use that).
Noise floorRoom/chain noise floor ≤ −60 dBFS at working gain (DIG-01 aims lower).
FIXED-GAIN setEvery variant recorded with the same preamp gain, marked with tape and logged. Why: the real level differences are the lesson — the cardioid's rear is quieter, distance drops 6 dB per doubling. Never normalize these files.
MATCHED setVariants loudness-matched to integrated LUFS within ±0.5 LU. Why: louder sounds “better” and brighter to everyone; removing level leaves only tone. How: make a separate COPY of the fixed-gain originals, apply a single static gain change per file (clip gain), nothing else; never alter the originals. Cap the gain at +20 dB (note any file that hits the cap).
LoopsSeamless; cut on bar lines at zero crossings. Tip: play the pattern three times and deliver the middle pass, so the first beat contains the natural ring-over from the bar before.
One-shotsKeep the full natural decay plus 0.5 s of room tone after it.
DRY roomTreated booth or dead room: RT60 ≤ 0.3 s, no audible early reflections.
SidecarOne row per delivered file in the folder's sidecars.csv (template below).
TakesSlate every take verbally and in the working filename (e.g. mpr01-cardioid-090_t02). Deliver the chosen take under the final name; put the take number in the sidecar.

Levels, loops and the two set types — drawn

Sidecar template (one sidecars.csv per lab folder)

Rights

  • Original recordings only, wholly owned by AP&E (work-for-hire or assignment in your contract).
  • Signed performer and voice releases for everyone heard, including babble volunteers and the remote podcast guest; location releases where needed.
  • No copyrighted songs, samples, loops or sound libraries. All music and lyrics are original (the house song, S2, the EP excerpts, the Northgate theme).
  • No recordings of the public with intelligible speech; no background music in field recordings.
  • No child voices without written guardian consent — the default is to skip them.

Delivery method

One folder per lab key, each with its sidecars.csv; manifest.csv at the top; signed releases in releases/; setup photos in photos/. Deliver as a single archive or shared drive folder; keep your session files and raw takes (including raw sweep recordings) archived for at least 12 months.

C · House scripts and music

S1 — spoken line (rich in plosives and sibilants)

“Peter's best microphone sits six inches from the speaker — simple, steady, and clear.”

Delivery: natural, conversational, about 4 s, even level, no performance colour. The same wording every time.

S2 — sung brief (original)

An original 8-bar melody whose lyric contains S, Z, SH, P and B. We recommend that S2 is the house song's lead vocal (A minor, 80 BPM, 8 bars): verse bars 1–4 soft, chorus bars 5–8 full voice. One song for everything means the singers learn one part.

Suggested lyric — suggested; the performer may substitute an original lyric meeting the same phoneme requirements:

Bars 1–2: Shadows pass the busy station,
Bars 3–4: silver buses hiss and sigh;
Bars 5–6: push the noise out, Sunday's breaking,
Bars 7–8: zip your coat and pass me by.

Contains S (station, silver, sigh, Sunday), Z (busy, buses, zip), SH (shadows, push), P (pass, push), B (busy, buses, breaking, by). Original text written for this brief.

Speech lists

  • Sustained vowels (3 s each, one pitch): AH (father) · EH (bed) · EE (see) · AW (law) · OO (boot).
  • Sustained voiced/unvoiced pairs (3 s each): SSS → ZZZ · FFF → VVV · SH → ZH (as in “measure”).
  • Consonant frames (“a_a”, one per second):
    Plosives: aPa · aBa · aTa · aDa · aKa · aGa
    Fricatives: aFa · aVa · aSa · aZa · aSHa · aZHa · aTHa (thin) · aTHa (this) · aHa
    Affricates: aCHa · aJa
    Nasals: aMa · aNa · aNGa
    Liquids: aLa · aRa
    Glides: aWa · aYa
  • Words: “professional audio”
  • De-Esser phrase: “This is a sentence with essess.”
  • Plosive line: “Bob bought a big blue bass.”
  • Line check: “Check one-two, sss, t-t-t.”
  • ADR line (PROD-03, original): “I told you the door was locked when I got here.”

The house song brief (original)

Key / tempoA minor, 80 BPM, 4/4
Length8 bars = exactly 24.000 s (1,152,000 samples at 48 kHz); loops seamlessly bar 8 → bar 1
FormVerse bars 1–4 (soft, intimate) into chorus bars 5–8 (full). The Mixing lab's automation page treats the first half as verse and the second half as chorus.
InstrumentationKick, snare, percussion (hi-hat + shaker), bass (DI + amp), electric guitar (comp/rhythm), keys/pad, lead vocal (S2), backing vocals (2–3 harmony parts).
Suggested harmonyVerse: Am | F | C | G — Chorus: F | G | Am | E (the E turns back to bar 1). Suggestion only; any original progression in A minor that loops works.
RecordingRecord to a click; play the 8-bar form three times without stopping and deliver the middle pass. No count-in in any delivered file. Every stem sample-aligned from bar 1 beat 1.
RightsWholly original music and lyric, owned by AP&E; no samples, loops or library sounds.

Reference speech passage — 30 s, phonetically balanced (original, 78 words)

When the sun rises over the harbor, the fishing boats are already out past the breakwater. Judy checks the weather while her brother Zack measures the rope and loads the heavy crates. Six gulls shout above the deck, and the cold spray stings their cheeks. By noon they will haul the nets, sort the catch, and choose which pieces to sell in the village market. It is tough, quiet work, yet they would not trade it for anything.

Original text written for this brief. Covers stops (P B T D K G), fricatives (F V S Z SH ZH TH H), affricates (CH J), nasals (M N NG), liquids, glides (W Y) and a wide vowel set. Read at about 150 words per minute (≈ 30 s).

“Northgate, episode 4” — scripted podcast, ≈ 60 s (original)

Cast: MAYA (host, studio), DAN (studio guest), SASHA (remote guest on a call). Names and places are fictional.

MAYA: Welcome back to Northgate. I'm Maya Ortiz, and this is episode four. Today we're talking about the old Palace Theatre on Bridge Street — and why it might open its doors again.

MAYA: With me in the studio is Dan Reyes, who runs the Northgate Preservation Project. Dan, thanks for coming in.

DAN: Happy to be here. People pass that building every day and probably picture a pile of plaster and pigeons. [plosive line]

MAYA: And joining us remotely is Sasha Lin, a structural engineer. Sasha, can you hear us?

SASHA: Loud and clear. I spent six weeks inspecting the place, and honestly, the steel is in surprisingly solid shape. [sibilance line]

DAN: That's the part nobody expects. The roof is the problem, not the bones.

MAYA: So what happens next?

SASHA: A proper survey, then a plan for the roof before winter.

MAYA: We'll pick that up after the break. Stay with us.

PROD-02 problems are recorded on these voices: the host plosive uses “Palace Theatre on Bridge Street”, the studio guest's plosive-rich line is “a pile of plaster and pigeons”, and the sibilant line is Sasha's “six weeks… surprisingly solid shape”.

About this lab page

Both Mixing labs (Beginning, 16 pages; Advanced, 20 pages) load one 8-track session. The learner balances, pans, EQs, compresses, sends to reverb and automates it on every page, from Build a Static Mix to The Final Mix. Today that session is a 10-second synthesized groove; the vocal and backing-vocal tracks are labelled on screen as a “synth stand-in for the vocal”.

Setup diagrams

Reuse: MIX-02 (same take), MIX-03, MST-01, EAR-01, EAR-03 bed feel, PATCH-01 (dry lead), MTR-01 music, SC-01, SS-04 (stems as monitor programme), Start Here.   See also: MIX-02 MST-01 FX-03

MIX-01.1 — Kick drum — inside/port close mic

3 files
Where it's used

Track 1 of the session and the first fader the learner sets on Build a Static Mix: the whole balance is built up from the kick. Later pages put a high-pass, a low-mid cut and a compressor on it, and set it against the bass for low-end space.

What it teaches

What a real close-miked kick contains: the low thump (50–100 Hz) that fights the bass, the cardboard low-mid (200–400 Hz) that EQ cleans out, and the beater click (2–5 kHz) that lets it cut through on small speakers. The synth kick has none of that detail.

What to record

The kick part of the house song, played by the drummer with the band to click.

How to make it
  1. Mic: large-diaphragm dynamic kick mic (Beta 52 / D112 class), cardioid.
  2. Placement: through the port into the drum, capsule 5–10 cm from the batter head, aimed at the beater but slightly off-centre (on-centre gives the most click, off-centre more body).
  3. Drum: tuned for a short, punchy note; a small pillow or blanket just touching the batter head. It should sound finished but untreated.
  4. Gain: hardest hit peaks around −8 dBFS so the loudest chorus fills stay under −6 dBFS.
  5. Capture: the band plays the 8-bar form (A minor, 80 BPM, verse bars 1–4, chorus bars 5–8) three times to click without stopping. Deliver the SECOND pass; cut at its downbeat, the same sample for all stems, so the file is exactly 1,152,000 samples and its first beat already contains the ring-over from the bar before (the loop has no hole).
  6. Master and both alternates come from three different full takes, never from different passes of one take.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Set the kick channel up first and leave it: ENV-01's single kick hit and MIX-02's kick-out mic use the same drum and tuning.
  • Tape the kick-mic stand to the floor: if it moves between takes, the alternates stop matching the master in tone.

MIX-01.2 — Snare — top close mic

3 files
Where it's used

The backbeat track. The learner EQs it (body vs crack), compresses it for snap and sends it to the reverb on the FX pages. On the Advanced Phase, Polarity and Alignment page it is the top half of the top/bottom pair (MIX-02.1 is the bottom).

What it teaches

The two parts of a snare: body at 150–250 Hz and crack at 2–5 kHz, plus the hi-hat bleed every real snare mic carries. A real snare shows how attack and release settings change the hit.

What to record

The snare part of the house song, close-miked on the top head.

How to make it
  1. Mic: cardioid dynamic (SM57 class).
  2. Placement: 3–5 cm above the rim at the drummer's side, angled 30–45° down toward the centre of the head; turn the mic so its rear (the null) points at the hi-hat.
  3. Snare: tuned medium, lightly damped (one gel pad at most), wires on.
  4. Gain: rim-shot accents peak around −8 dBFS.
  5. Capture: the band plays the 8-bar form (A minor, 80 BPM, verse bars 1–4, chorus bars 5–8) three times to click without stopping. Deliver the SECOND pass; cut at its downbeat, the same sample for all stems, so the file is exactly 1,152,000 samples and its first beat already contains the ring-over from the bar before (the loop has no hole).
  6. Master and both alternates come from three different full takes, never from different passes of one take.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Leave the polarity exactly as it comes from the mic: MIX-02.1 (snare bottom) is judged against this track.
  • This same mic and tuning give ENV-01's single snare hit: record that one-shot during the drum setup, before the band arrives.

MIX-01.3 — Percussion — hi-hat and shaker on one SDC

3 files
Where it's used

The top-end rhythm track. The learner pans it off-centre, high-passes it and turns it down until it sits under the vocal; it is also the track that shows how much high end a mix really needs.

What it teaches

A high, busy part needs little level and no low end: a high-pass up to 300–500 Hz removes kick and snare bleed without changing the part. Panning it moves the whole mix's top end.

What to record

Hi-hat played by the drummer and a shaker played by a second percussionist, both into one small-diaphragm condenser.

How to make it
  1. Mic: cardioid small-diaphragm condenser (SDC).
  2. Placement: 15 cm above the hi-hat, aimed between the edge and the bell, angled away from the snare.
  3. Shaker: the percussionist stands 30 cm from the same SDC, on-axis, and plays 16ths through the chorus (bars 5–8) only, or throughout if the arrangement calls for it; note which in the sidecar.
  4. Gain: hi-hat accents peak around −10 dBFS.
  5. Capture: the band plays the 8-bar form (A minor, 80 BPM, verse bars 1–4, chorus bars 5–8) three times to click without stopping. Deliver the SECOND pass; cut at its downbeat, the same sample for all stems, so the file is exactly 1,152,000 samples and its first beat already contains the ring-over from the bar before (the loop has no hole).
  6. Master and both alternates come from three different full takes, never from different passes of one take.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • If the shaker is overdubbed instead, do it to the master drum take, then to each alternate take, so all three files still line up with their own takes.
  • Keep the hi-hat mic out of the snare's direct line: snare bleed here makes the high-pass lesson less clean.

MIX-01.4 — Bass — DI

3 files
Where it's used

The low-end partner of the kick. The learner balances the two, compresses the bass to even out the notes, and carves EQ space between bass and kick. On the Advanced Phase page it is the DI half of the DI/amp pair (MIX-02.3).

What it teaches

A clean DI bass: full, even low end with no room and no amp colour, so the fight with the kick at 50–100 Hz is easy to see and hear. Real finger dynamics show what a compressor is for.

What to record

The bass part played by the bassist with the band, taken from a DI box before the amp.

How to make it
  1. DI: active DI box; bass into the DI input, DI thru to the bass amp (MIX-02.3 mics that amp at the same time).
  2. Ground lift off unless there is hum; if it is used, note it.
  3. Bassist plays with consistent fingers or pick throughout all three takes; tell them to play the part, not to compress themselves.
  4. Gain: loudest notes peak around −8 dBFS.
  5. Capture: the band plays the 8-bar form (A minor, 80 BPM, verse bars 1–4, chorus bars 5–8) three times to click without stopping. Deliver the SECOND pass; cut at its downbeat, the same sample for all stems, so the file is exactly 1,152,000 samples and its first beat already contains the ring-over from the bar before (the loop has no hole).
  6. Master and both alternates come from three different full takes, never from different passes of one take.
Diagram
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Print DI and amp mic from the same DI box on the same take: that is what makes the Advanced Phase page work.
  • Fresh-ish strings: dead strings make the DI dull and the EQ lesson harder.

MIX-01.5 — Electric guitar — close mic on the amp

3 files
Where it's used

The mid-range track. The learner pans it, high-passes it and cuts room for the vocal in the 1–4 kHz region; on the Advanced pages it pairs with the guitar room mic (MIX-02.6).

What it teaches

Masking: a real guitar and a real vocal share 1–4 kHz, so the vocal disappears when the guitar is loud there. Small EQ cuts and panning bring the vocal back without turning the guitar down.

What to record

The rhythm-guitar part, close-miked on the amp.

How to make it
  1. Mic: cardioid dynamic (SM57 class).
  2. Placement: 3 cm from the grille cloth, on-axis to the cone just off the dust cap (on the cap is brighter, further out is darker; note the spot).
  3. Amp: a clean-to-edge-of-breakup tone, not heavily distorted; volume moderate.
  4. Gain: loudest strums peak around −8 dBFS.
  5. Capture: the band plays the 8-bar form (A minor, 80 BPM, verse bars 1–4, chorus bars 5–8) three times to click without stopping. Deliver the SECOND pass; cut at its downbeat, the same sample for all stems, so the file is exactly 1,152,000 samples and its first beat already contains the ring-over from the bar before (the loop has no hole).
  6. Master and both alternates come from three different full takes, never from different passes of one take.
Diagram
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Mark the mic position on the grille cloth with tape: the alternates must sound like the same mic position.
  • MIX-02.6 (the room mic) is up at the same time; set it before the first take.

MIX-01.6 — Keys / pad

3 files
Where it's used

The sustained harmonic bed. The learner fits it under the vocal with EQ and level, and automates it between verse and chorus.

What it teaches

A pad fills the same mid-range the vocal needs; turning it down is the wrong first move — a gentle cut where the vocal lives keeps the pad's size and lets the voice through.

What to record

The keyboard part, recorded direct.

How to make it
  1. Source: the keyboard's stereo outputs summed to mono at the DI, or the LEFT output only if the patch is mono-compatible. Write which in the sidecar.
  2. Patch: a warm pad or electric-piano/pad layer with no built-in delay or chorus on the output (effects belong to the mix lab).
  3. Gain: loudest chords peak around −8 dBFS.
  4. Capture: the band plays the 8-bar form (A minor, 80 BPM, verse bars 1–4, chorus bars 5–8) three times to click without stopping. Deliver the SECOND pass; cut at its downbeat, the same sample for all stems, so the file is exactly 1,152,000 samples and its first beat already contains the ring-over from the bar before (the loop has no hole).
  5. Master and both alternates come from three different full takes, never from different passes of one take.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Check the mono sum before the first take: some stereo patches cancel when summed. Switch to the left output if they do.
  • Ask the player to keep the same voicings across all three takes.

MIX-01.7 — Lead vocal — S2, soft verse into full chorus

3 files
Where it's used

The track the whole mix serves. The learner sets it on top of the band, compresses and de-esses it, sends it to reverb and, on the automation page, rides it up from the soft verse (first half) into the loud chorus (second half). Today it is a synth stand-in.

What it teaches

Mixing a real voice: real sibilance to tame, real verse-to-chorus dynamics to automate, and real masking by the guitar and keys. The lesson only works if the performance itself gets louder in the chorus.

What to record

The S2 melody and lyric (contains S, Z, SH, P and B), sung over the band take: soft and intimate in bars 1–4, full voice in bars 5–8.

How to make it
  1. Overdub in the booth to the drum, bass, guitar and keys take, after the band is done.
  2. Mic: cardioid large-diaphragm condenser (LDC) at 15–20 cm, mouth height, with a fabric pop filter 5 cm in front of the grille.
  3. Room: DRY booth. Headphones closed-back and not too loud, to keep click and band spill out of the mic.
  4. Gain: set on the loudest chorus note, peaking around −8 dBFS; leave it fixed through all takes.
  5. Performance: real dynamics — no leaning into the mic in the chorus to compensate; the level change must come from the voice.
  6. Sing over each of the three band takes; cut each vocal with its band take.
  7. Master and both alternates come from three different full takes, never from different passes of one take.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Comp nothing: each delivered file is one continuous vocal pass, so the de-esser and compressor see a real performance.
  • Mute the click in the singer's headphones if it bleeds; give them the drums instead.
  • Record DES-01 and EQ-01 vocal items with the same singer on the same day while the voice is warm.

MIX-01.8 — Backing vocals — 2–3 harmony parts bounced to one mono file

3 files
Where it's used

The support vocal track. The learner sets it behind the lead with level, a darker EQ, more reverb and, on the Advanced pages, group compression.

What it teaches

Backing vocals sit behind the lead: lower, darker and more distant, so the lead stays in front. A real stack of voices also shows why one bus compressor glues them together.

What to record

Two or three harmony parts to the chorus (and verse if arranged), each sung once, balanced and bounced to one mono file.

How to make it
  1. Same booth, LDC and pop filter as the lead; singers at 30 cm (further than the lead, so the parts sound slightly more distant).
  2. Record each harmony part as its own pass over each band take, then bounce the parts to one mono file at a simple balance. Level only: no EQ, compression or reverb.
  3. Master and both alternates come from three different full takes, never from different passes of one take.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record the backing parts right after the lead while the singer is warm; if the same singer sings them, keep the distance at 30 cm so the parts sound different from the lead.
  • Keep the harmony parts' individual files in your archive; deliver only the bounce.

About this lab page

MIX-02.1 — Snare — bottom mic (polarity as recorded)

1 file
Where it's used

Paired with the snare top (MIX-01.2) on Phase, Polarity and Alignment. The learner sums the two, hears the snare go thin, presses Ø on the bottom mic and hears it come back full.

What it teaches

Two mics facing each other on one drum head see opposite pressure: the bottom head moves away when the top moves toward the top mic. Summed as recorded they partly cancel; flipping one restores the body. That is a polarity lesson, not a timing one.

What to record

The snare wires captured from underneath, on the MIX-01 takes.

How to make it
  1. Mic: cardioid dynamic or SDC.
  2. Placement: 5–8 cm under the snare, pointing up at the wires, angled away from the kick beater.
  3. Leave the polarity exactly as the mic delivers it; no Ø switch on the preamp.
  4. Gain: peaks around −10 dBFS (it is brighter and spikier than the top).
  5. Set this mic up before the first MIX-01 take: it rides on the same three takes and is cut at the same sample as the MIX-01 stems.
  6. Measure the top/bottom time offset from a single hit and write it in the offsets sidecar.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Never polarity-correct or align it: the thin sum is the lesson.
  • If the preamp has a Ø button, tape over it.

  • Wires are bright and clear; kick bleed is audible but not dominant.

MIX-02.2 — Kick — outside mic, 20 cm from the front head

1 file
Where it's used

Paired with the kick-inside mic (MIX-01.1) on Phase, Polarity and Alignment. The learner sums them, hears comb-filter colour, then nudges the inside mic later in time until the low end locks.

What it teaches

Two mics at different distances from one source arrive at different times: about 0.6 ms later per 20 cm. The sum comb-filters (some frequencies cancel, some add) until the earlier mic is delayed to match. This is a timing lesson, unlike the snare bottom.

What to record

The kick from outside the front head, on the MIX-01 takes.

How to make it
  1. Mic: LDC or large dynamic, cardioid.
  2. Placement: 20 cm outside the front (resonant) head, on-axis with the beater; if the head has a port, aim at the solid head beside it.
  3. Gain: peaks around −10 dBFS.
  4. Set this mic up before the first MIX-01 take: it rides on the same three takes and is cut at the same sample as the MIX-01 stems.
  5. Measure the inside/outside offset from a single hit and write it in the offsets sidecar.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Never time-align it to the inside mic: the comb filter is the lesson.
  • A short tunnel (blanket over the mic and drum) cuts cymbal spill if the room is live; note it.

MIX-02.3 — Bass — amp mic (same take as the DI)

1 file
Where it's used

Paired with the bass DI (MIX-01.4) on the Advanced Phase page and on Stems and Alternate Mixes. The learner blends DI and amp, hears the blend go hollow, and aligns the amp to the DI.

What it teaches

An amp mic arrives later than its DI: the speaker, the air gap and converter latency add a fraction of a millisecond to a few milliseconds. Blending the two without alignment thins the low end; aligned, the DI gives the floor and the amp gives the growl.

What to record

The bass amp's speaker, miked on the same take as the DI.

How to make it
  1. Mic: cardioid dynamic or LDC.
  2. Placement: 5–10 cm from the speaker cone, slightly off the centre.
  3. Signal: from the DI box's thru output; the DI is the MIX-01.4 stem.
  4. Gain: peaks around −8 dBFS.
  5. Set this mic up before the first MIX-01 take: it rides on the same three takes and is cut at the same sample as the MIX-01 stems.
  6. Measure DI-to-amp offset from a single plucked note and write it in the offsets sidecar.
Diagram
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Do not align or polarity-flip the amp track; that is the learner's job.
  • Keep the amp at a moderate level so it does not bleed into the drum mics more than a real session would.

MIX-02.4 — Drum overheads — spaced pair or ORTF, left and right

2 files
Where it's used

The kit picture on Advanced Dynamics and Stem Reconstruction: the learner hears how much of every drum the overheads carry, and why gating the close mics changes the kit sound less than expected. The two files are the two halves of one stereo pair.

What it teaches

Overheads are the whole kit at a distance: cymbals plus every drum arriving a few milliseconds after the close mics. They show bleed as part of the sound, not a fault, and they set the stereo picture of the kit.

What to record

The whole kit from above with a matched stereo pair, delivered as two mono files (left, right).

How to make it
  1. Mics: matched pair of cardioid SDCs.
  2. Placement: spaced pair or ORTF about 1 m above the cymbals; measure the distance from each capsule to the centre of the snare and make them equal (tape measure). Note the technique and the distances.
  3. Gain: identical on both channels; crash hits peak around −8 dBFS.
  4. Set this mic up before the first MIX-01 take: it rides on the same three takes and is cut at the same sample as the MIX-01 stems.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Equal distance to the snare is what keeps the snare centred; check it with a tape measure, not by eye.
  • Photograph the kit and overheads from above and from the front for the delivery folder.

MIX-02.5 — Drum room — stereo pair 3–4 m from the kit

2 files
Where it's used

The ambience tracks on Advanced Dynamics and Stem Reconstruction. The learner blends the room under the close mics, compresses it hard for size, and hears it arrive later than everything else.

What it teaches

A room pair gives size and distance; it arrives about 9–12 ms after the close mics at 3–4 m, so it adds depth rather than detail. Heavy compression on it makes the kit sound bigger without changing the close mics.

What to record

The whole kit in the room from 3–4 m, with a stereo pair delivered as two mono files.

How to make it
  1. Mics: matched pair (cardioid LDCs or omnis).
  2. Placement: 3–4 m in front of the kit at head height, about 1–2 m apart, facing the kit.
  3. Gain: identical on both channels; loudest fills peak around −8 dBFS.
  4. Set this mic up before the first MIX-01 take: it rides on the same three takes and is cut at the same sample as the MIX-01 stems.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Walk the room while the drummer plays and put the pair where the kit sounds best, not where it is convenient.
  • Keep the bass amp turned away from the room pair.

MIX-02.6 — Electric guitar — room mic 1.5–2 m

1 file
Where it's used

Paired with the close guitar (MIX-01.5) on Phase, Polarity and Alignment and on Stems and Alternate Mixes: the learner blends close and room, hears the delay, and decides whether to align it.

What it teaches

A distant mic on the same amp arrives 4–6 ms late and carries the room. Blended under the close mic it adds space; aligned, it thickens instead. Both are valid choices, and the learner hears the difference.

What to record

The guitar amp from 1.5–2 m away in the room.

How to make it
  1. Mic: cardioid LDC or omni.
  2. Placement: 1.5–2 m from the amp, at the height of the speaker, facing it.
  3. Gain: peaks around −10 dBFS.
  4. Set this mic up before the first MIX-01 take: it rides on the same three takes and is cut at the same sample as the MIX-01 stems.
  5. Measure the close-to-room offset from a single pick attack and write it in the offsets sidecar.
Diagram
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Do not align it to the close mic.
  • If the drums bleed heavily, move the mic closer to the amp (not further than 2 m) and note the distance.

MIX-03.1 — Clean professional mix (the reference)

1 file
Where it's used

The target on every check-and-finish page: the learner's own mix and the three flawed bounces are all compared against it.

What it teaches

What a finished, translated mix of this song sounds like: vocal on top, kick and bass locked, nothing harsh or muddy, and level that holds up on a phone and on monitors.

What to record

A professional mix of MIX-01 (stems plus MIX-02 mics), lightly mastered.

How to make it
  1. Mix MIX-01 with the MIX-02 mics to a clean, professional balance. EQ, compression, reverb and limiting ARE allowed here: this item is a produced mix.
  2. Master lightly to −14 LUFS integrated and ≤ −1 dBTP.
  3. Bounce the same 24.000 s loop as MIX-01. Write every processing setting in the sidecar.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Check it on a phone speaker and in a car or earbuds before calling it done: it is the translation reference.
  • Keep this session: the three flawed versions are made from it.

MIX-03.2 — Flawed mix: HARSH (+4 dB high shelf at 3 kHz)

1 file
Where it's used

One of the three flawed bounces on the check pages: the learner A/Bs it with the clean mix at the same loudness and names the fault.

What it teaches

Harshness: too much 3 kHz and above makes cymbals and S sounds hurt and the mix tiring, even at the same loudness. It is the most common translation failure on phone speakers and earbuds.

What to record

The clean mix with one extra high shelf on the stereo bus.

How to make it
  1. Start from the clean pro mix session (MIX-03.1). Change ONLY the one setting below, then bounce.
  2. Add a +4 dB high shelf at 3 kHz on the master bus, before the limiter.
  3. Loudness-match to the clean version within ±0.5 LU.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Bounce all four from one session so nothing else changes.

MIX-03.3 — Flawed mix: MUDDY (low-mid build-up)

1 file
Where it's used

The second flawed bounce: the learner hears a mix that is the same loudness but cloudy, and names the low-mids as the cause.

What it teaches

Mud: a build-up around 200–300 Hz blurs the kick, bass and guitar together and buries the vocal's clarity, without making anything louder.

What to record

The clean mix with one wide low-mid boost on the stereo bus.

How to make it
  1. Start from the clean pro mix session (MIX-03.1). Change ONLY the one setting below, then bounce.
  2. Suggested: +4 dB wide bell, Q about 0.7, at 250 Hz on the master bus, before the limiter.
  3. Loudness-match to the clean version within ±0.5 LU.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • If the suggested boost is not obvious on a phone, raise it to +5 dB and note the setting.

MIX-03.4 — Flawed mix: OVER-COMPRESSED (pumping)

1 file
Where it's used

The third flawed bounce: matched in loudness, so the learner judges the squashed dynamics and pumping, not the level.

What it teaches

Over-compression flattens the drums' attack, makes the mix pump with the kick, and kills the verse-to-chorus lift. At matched loudness it sounds smaller, not bigger.

What to record

The clean mix through heavy bus compression.

How to make it
  1. Start from the clean pro mix session (MIX-03.1). Change ONLY the one setting below, then bounce.
  2. Suggested: heavy bus compression, fast attack and release, audible pumping; push it until the crest factor is about 6 dB.
  3. Loudness-match to the clean version within ±0.5 LU.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Measure the crest factor (peak minus RMS) and write it in the sidecar next to the clean mix's value.

MST-01.1 — Unmastered mix — no bus processing

1 file
Where it's used

The programme that plays through the whole Mastering rack. The learner adds tilt EQ, limiting and width to it and A/Bs at matched level; it is also the “bus-limiter-off” mix Module 8 tells them to ask for.

What it teaches

What a mastering engineer wants to receive: a balanced mix with headroom and intact transients, so small tilt EQ moves and the limiter's effect on the drums are clearly audible.

What to record

A balanced stereo mix of the MIX-01 song with no processing on the stereo bus.

How to make it
  1. Mix MIX-01 (with the MIX-02 mics) to a balanced, finished-sounding mix. Channel processing is fine; the stereo bus has NOTHING on it (no EQ, compressor or limiter).
  2. Set the master fader so the sample peak is about −4 dBFS; that gives about −19 LUFS integrated and a peak-to-loudness ratio (PLR) of about 15 dB.
  3. Bounce the same 24.000 s loop as MIX-01.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Print MST-01.2 from this exact session straight afterwards, so the limiter is the only difference.
  • After bouncing, convert a test copy to 44.1 kHz with a high-quality converter and check it does not clip; discard the test copy.

MST-01.2 — Bus-limited mix — same mix through a limiter

1 file
Where it's used

The version a mix engineer often sends by mistake. In Module 8 the learner compares it with MST-01.1 and learns why a mastering engineer asks for the mix with the bus limiter off.

What it teaches

A bus limiter already used up the headroom: it is louder (≈ −12.6 vs ≈ −19 LUFS) but the transients are flattened, so the mastering limiter has nothing left to work with. At matched loudness it sounds smaller than the unmastered mix.

What to record

The MST-01.1 mix with a limiter on the stereo bus.

How to make it
  1. Open the MST-01.1 session. Add one true-peak limiter on the stereo bus, ceiling −0.1 dBTP, input driven until the integrated loudness is about −12.6 LUFS.
  2. Change nothing else. Bounce the same 24.000 s loop.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Write the limiter model and settings in the sidecar.
  • Check the 44.1 kHz test copy for inter-sample overs; adjust the ceiling only if it clips, and note it.

About this lab page

Mic Principles › Pickup Patterns and Off-Axis Response. The learner picks a pattern (omni, cardioid, super, hyper, figure-8) and drags a source around the mic, or sweeps an ANGLE fader 0–180° with preset chips at 0°, 30°, 60°, 90° and 180°. The polar plot and readouts move. Today the page is silent.

Setup diagram

Safety: SAFE-3 for phantom power when changing mics (switch phantom off before plugging). (Safety section)

Reuse: Speech off-axis (SPC-04 records its own take — see there), Mic Selection, Spectrogram demo.   See also: MPR-03 SPC-04 MSL-01

MPR-01.1 — Omni — on-axis — the reference for the whole set

2 files
Where it's used

Plays on Mic Principles › Pickup Patterns / Off-Axis Response when PATTERN = OMNI and the source sits at on-axis — the reference for the whole set (a preset ANGLE chip). The learner compares it with the other angles of the same pattern; the MATCHED copy lets them hear the tone change with the level difference removed.

What it teaches

The level and tone every other take in MPR-01 is judged against. An omni at 30 cm in a dry booth: natural, full, with no proximity boost. Theory for this position: 0 dB (reference).

What to record

S1 spoken by the house adult male voice; multi-pattern LDC on omni, mic rotated to 0° from the mouth at 30 cm.

How to make it
  1. Room: DRY booth (RT60 ≤ 0.3 s). Talker seated, head against a headrest marker so the mouth never moves. Mic at mouth height, capsule centre 30 cm from the lips at 0°.
  2. Tape a printed 360° protractor to the floor, centred under the capsule (use a plumb line). Rotate the MIC about the vertical axis through its capsule; the talker never turns.
  3. Mic: a C414-class multi-pattern LDC. If it has no named supercardioid, use the position between cardioid and hypercardioid and say so in the sidecar.
  4. Reference mic: any cardioid at 30 cm on-axis on a spare channel, never moved, never delivered. It shows how loud the talker was on each take.
  5. Gain: set ONCE, on omni at 0° (this take), so S1 peaks around −6 dBFS. Tape the knob. Never touch it for all 27 positions.
  6. Two takes of S1 per position, slated (“pattern omni, zero degrees, take one”). Keep the take whose reference-mic level is closest to the omni-0° take (reject drift over 0.5 dB).
  7. Order: one pattern at a time — 0°, 30°, 60°, 90°, (null), 180° — then change pattern; 20 s of room tone at the end of each pattern block.
  8. MATCHED copy: loudness-match the kept take to the omni-0° take within ±0.5 LU, but never apply more than +20 dB; if it needs more, stop at +20 dB and note it.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record this first: it sets the gain for all 27 positions.
  • Rotate the mic, not the talker: a mouth is directional too, so turning the head would change the sound for the wrong reason.
  • Batch all angles before changing pattern — pattern switching on some LDCs needs a few seconds to settle.

MPR-01.2 — Omni — 30°

2 files
Where it's used

What it teaches

An omni does not care about 30°: same level, same tone as 0°. This is what “omni” means — no rejection, so no penalty for a talker who moves. Theory for this position: ≈ 0 dB.

Plays on Mic Principles › Pickup Patterns / Off-Axis Response when PATTERN = OMNI and the source sits at 180°, rear (a preset ANGLE chip). The learner compares it with the other angles of the same pattern; the MATCHED copy lets them hear the tone change with the level difference removed.

What it teaches

An omni has no null: the voice from behind is nearly as loud as from the front, only a little duller from the mic body's shadow. This is why an omni gives no protection from a monitor wedge behind it. Theory for this position: ≈ 0 dB (body shadow on the highs).

What to record

S1 spoken by the house adult male voice; multi-pattern LDC on omni, mic rotated to 180° from the mouth at 30 cm.

How to make it
  1. Same rig, talker position and taped gain as MPR-01.1. Pattern: omni. Rotate the mic about its capsule to 180° on the floor protractor.
  2. MATCHED copy: loudness-match the kept take to the omni-0° take within ±0.5 LU, but never apply more than +20 dB; if it needs more, stop at +20 dB and note it.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Watch the reference mic: if the talker drifts more than 0.5 dB from the omni-0° take, take it again.

MPR-01.21 — Hypercardioid — the null, ≈110°

2 files
Where it's used

Plays on Mic Principles › Pickup Patterns / Off-Axis Response when PATTERN = HYPERCARDIOID and the source sits at the null, ≈110° (between the ANGLE chips — reached by dragging the source around the polar plot). The learner compares it with the other angles of the same pattern; the MATCHED copy lets them hear the tone change with the level difference removed.

What it teaches

The hypercardioid's null is at about 110°, even further forward than the super's. Monitors for a hyper go to the side-rear, never directly behind. Theory for this position: null (≈110° in theory — use the measured angle).

What to record

S1 spoken by the house adult male voice; multi-pattern LDC on hypercardioid, mic rotated to 110° from the mouth at 30 cm.

How to make it
  1. Same rig, talker position and taped gain as MPR-01.1. Pattern: hypercardioid. Rotate the mic about its capsule to 110° on the floor protractor.
  2. Find the real null with pink noise from the talker position, as for the super; record at the MEASURED angle (theory ≈110°).
  3. MATCHED copy: loudness-match the kept take to the omni-0° take within ±0.5 LU, but never apply more than +20 dB; if it needs more, stop at +20 dB and note it.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • The file name keeps 110 even if the measured null differs; the true angle goes in the sidecar.
  • Watch the reference mic: if the talker drifts more than 0.5 dB from the omni-0° take, take it again.

The figure-8's side null is the deepest and most reliable null of any pattern: it is what makes the side mic of M/S and Blumlein pairs work, and how a ribbon rejects a source beside it. Theory for this position: null (deepest, most reliable null).

About this lab page

Mic Principles › Distance & the Room. The learner drags a DISTANCE fader from 4 to 48 inches; readouts show level relative to 4 in and the percentage of direct sound. Today it is silent.

Reuse: Speech › The Distance Effect (context), Wave reverb, Gain lab.   See also: SPC-04 MPR-01

MPR-02.1 — Male voice · cardioid dynamic · 4 in

1 file
Where it's used

Mic Principles › Distance and the Room with the DISTANCE fader at 4 in (readouts: LEVEL 0 dB rel 4 in, DIRECT 90%). This is the male voice on the cardioid dynamic; the other voice and the other mic at the same mark give the page a second voice and a second pickup pattern at the same distance.

What it teaches

The reference: the direct voice dominates (about 90% of what the mic hears in the app's model). Close, intimate and dry, even in a live room. The cardioid rejects some of the room from behind, so it stays drier than the omni at the same distance. At 4–6 in the dynamic also adds proximity warmth that the omni does not.

What to record

S1 by the male voice on the cardioid dynamic (SM58 class), mouth to capsule 4 in, untreated medium room.

How to make it
  1. Room: an untreated medium room, RT60 about 0.6–0.8 s (NOT the booth). Talker standing in the middle of the room, away from walls.
  2. Mount the cardioid dynamic and the omni side by side on one stand bar, capsules touching; both record at once.
  3. Mark 4, 6, 12, 24 and 48 in on the floor with tape, measured mouth to capsule.
  4. Set each preamp's gain once at 4 in so S1 peaks around −6 dBFS. Tape the knobs. Do not touch them for any distance or for the second voice.
  5. Use a fixed reference mic (as in MPR-01) to keep the talker's voice level steady; redo any take that drifts more than 0.5 dB.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Capture both mics in one performance — halves the session and guarantees the same delivery.
  • Do the female voice straight after the male without moving the stand marks.

MPR-02.4 — Male voice · cardioid dynamic · 24 in

1 file
Where it's used

Mic Principles › Distance and the Room with the DISTANCE fader at 24 in (readouts: LEVEL ≈ −15.6 dB rel 4 in, DIRECT 20%). This is the male voice on the cardioid dynamic; the other voice and the other mic at the same mark give the page a second voice and a second pickup pattern at the same distance.

What it teaches

The room has taken over: the voice sounds distant and hollow, and turning the gain up only brings up more room. The cardioid rejects some of the room from behind, so it stays drier than the omni at the same distance.

What to record

S1 by the male voice on the cardioid dynamic (SM58 class), mouth to capsule 24 in, untreated medium room.

How to make it
  1. Same room, stand bar and taped gains as MPR-02.1; stand moved to the 24 in mark. The talker stays put and keeps the same voice level.
  2. This is the cardioid dynamic channel of the side-by-side pair: it comes from the same performance as the other mic's 24 in take.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Never normalise: the level drop from 4 in is the lesson.

Mic Principles › Distance and the Room with the DISTANCE fader at 48 in (readouts: LEVEL ≈ −21.6 dB rel 4 in, DIRECT 6%). This is the female voice on the omni; the other voice and the other mic at the same mark give the page a second voice and a second pickup pattern at the same distance.

What it teaches

Mostly room: the voice is far away, smeared by reflections, and the room's noise floor becomes part of the sound. The omni hears the room from every direction, so at the same distance it always sounds roomier than the cardioid.

What to record

S1 by the female voice on the omni, mouth to capsule 48 in, untreated medium room.

How to make it
  1. Same room, stand bar and taped gains as MPR-02.1; stand moved to the 48 in mark. The talker stays put and keeps the same voice level.
  2. This is the omni channel of the side-by-side pair: it comes from the same performance as the other mic's 48 in take.
  3. Record 20 s of room tone at the 48 in position (once per voice).
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Never normalise: the level drop from 4 in is the lesson.

MPR-03Proximity effect — cardioid versus omniP1Session 120 recordings · 40 files
P1 Session 1 · 20 recordings · 40 files

About this lab page

Mic Principles › Proximity Effect. The learner drags DISTANCE from 12 in down to 1 in and switches MIC between CARDIOID and OMNI; the readout shows the low-shelf boost (up to about +10 dB at 1–2 in on cardioid; none on omni). Today it is silent.

Setup diagram

MPR-03.1 — S1 spoken · cardioid dynamic · 1 in

2 files
Where it's used

Mic Principles › Proximity Effect with DISTANCE = 1 in and MIC = CARDIOID (readout: +10 dB). The learner steps from 12 in down to 1 in and flips between the two mics; the spoken version shows it on a natural voice.

What it teaches

Maximum proximity effect: the cardioid's low end is boosted by about 10 dB. Even loudness-matched it is much fuller and boomier than at 12 in — a tone change, not just a level change. On speech the boost shows as chest and boom under the words, and it makes the plosives heavier.

What to record

S1 spoken by the low male voice, on the cardioid dynamic, 1 in from lips to grille.

How to make it
  1. Room: DRY booth. Talker seated, head on a headrest marker; mic on a stand at mouth height, on-axis.
  2. Mics: a cardioid dynamic and a TRUE pressure omni (not a multi-pattern LDC on omni — its two-diaphragm omni can still show some proximity).
  3. Gain: set on each mic at 1 in so the loudest plosive peaks no higher than −3 dBFS. Tape the knob.
  4. Record 12 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 in on the cardioid, then switch mics and repeat. Measure lips to grille with a ruler every time.
  5. MATCHED copy: loudness-match to the 12 in take of the same mic and source within ±0.5 LU.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Plosives will be strong this close: keep them (they are real); if a take clips, redo it at the same gain with a slightly softer P.
  • The MATCHED copies are what let learners hear that “bassier” is not just “louder”.
  • Record the whole distance ladder for one mic and source in one run, without touching the stand height.

MPR-03.6 — S1 spoken · true omni · 1 in

2 files
Where it's used

Mic Principles › Proximity Effect with DISTANCE = 1 in and MIC = OMNI (readout: FLAT). The learner steps from 12 in down to 1 in and flips between the two mics; the spoken version shows it on a natural voice.

An omni at 1 in: much LOUDER than at 12 in, but in the MATCHED copy the tone is the same. A pressure mic has no gradient, so no proximity effect — the app's readout says FLAT. On speech the boost shows as chest and boom under the words, and it makes the plosives heavier.

MPR-03.11 — Sung A2 (110 Hz) · cardioid dynamic · 1 in

2 files
Where it's used

Mic Principles › Proximity Effect with DISTANCE = 1 in and MIC = CARDIOID (readout: +10 dB). The learner steps from 12 in down to 1 in and flips between the two mics; the sung-note version makes the low-end change easiest to hear.

What it teaches

Maximum proximity effect: the cardioid's low end is boosted by about 10 dB. Even loudness-matched it is much fuller and boomier than at 12 in — a tone change, not just a level change. A steady 110 Hz note puts the fundamental right inside the proximity region, so the boost is easiest to hear and to see on an analyser.

What to record

A sung A2 (110 Hz) held on “ah” for 4 s by the same low male singer, on the cardioid dynamic, 1 in from lips to grille.

How to make it
  1. Same booth, headrest and taped cardioid dynamic gain as MPR-03.1. Ruler-measure 1 in from lips to grille, on-axis.
  2. Give the singer A2 (110 Hz) from a tuner drone in one headphone ear; hold “ah” for 4 s, steady, no vibrato.
  3. MATCHED copy: loudness-match to the 12 in take of the same mic and source within ±0.5 LU.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Plosives will be strong this close: keep them (they are real); if a take clips, redo it at the same gain with a slightly softer P.
  • Record the whole distance ladder for one mic and source in one run, without touching the stand height.

Proximity effect building as the cardioid moves in: about ≈ +2.4 dB of low-shelf lift against 12 in (app model). The closer, the bassier. A steady 110 Hz note puts the fundamental right inside the proximity region, so the boost is easiest to hear and to see on an analyser.

MPR-04aPlosives: no protection, pop filter, foamP1Session 16 recordings · 6 files
P1 Session 1 · 6 recordings · 6 files

About this lab page

Mic Principles › Plosives & Wind. A BARRIER tray offers NONE, POP FILTER, FOAM and SHOTGUN WINDSHIELD; a readout shows how much of the blast reaches the capsule (100% / 30% / 50% / 12%). This item covers the indoor plosive part (NONE, POP FILTER, FOAM). Today it is silent.

Setup diagram

Reuse: Speech › Why Pop Filters Work, EQ high-pass context.   See also: MPR-04b SPC-04 PROD-02

Recordings in this item: MPR-04a.1 MPR-04a.2 MPR-04a.3 MPR-04a.4 MPR-04a.5 MPR-04a.6

MPR-04a.1 — Large-diaphragm condenser — no protection

1 file
Where it's used

Mic Principles › Plosives and Wind with the BARRIER tray on NONE (readout: 100% of the blast reaches the capsule). This is the large-diaphragm condenser version; the learner compares it with the other two barriers on the same mic.

What it teaches

The light condenser diaphragm takes the full air blast: the P and B in both lines arrive as huge slow low-frequency thumps, far bigger than the words. This is the 100% case on the tray.

What to record

The plosive lines “Peter's best microphone sits six inches from the speaker — simple, steady, and clear.” followed by “Bob bought a big blue bass.”, spoken at 2–3 in on the LDC, none.

How to make it
  1. DRY booth. Talker standing or seated, mouth 2–3 in from the grille, on-axis, at mouth height. One take contains both lines; same energy on every P and B.
  2. NO filter, no foam. Set the gain HERE so the worst pop peaks at −3 dBFS; tape it and keep it for the LDC pop-filter and foam takes.
  3. Record this one LAST for the LDC (see tips), but set the gain on a trial run of it first.
  4. Slate each take with the mic and barrier.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record the NONE take last for each mic — a bad pop can momentarily overload a condenser capsule; get the protected takes in the can first.
  • Watch the waveform: a real plosive shows one slow, huge low-frequency swing. That is what you are capturing.

MPR-04a.2 — Large-diaphragm condenser — pop filter

1 file
Where it's used

Mic Principles › Plosives and Wind with the BARRIER tray on POP FILTER (readout: 30%). This is the large-diaphragm condenser version; the learner compares it with the other two barriers on the same mic.

What it teaches

The mesh breaks up the air burst before it reaches the capsule; the voice passes untouched. The thumps disappear and the consonants stay crisp (the app reads about 30% of the blast getting through).

What to record

The plosive lines “Peter's best microphone sits six inches from the speaker — simple, steady, and clear.” followed by “Bob bought a big blue bass.”, spoken at 2–3 in on the LDC, pop filter.

How to make it
  1. DRY booth. Talker standing or seated, mouth 2–3 in from the grille, on-axis, at mouth height. One take contains both lines; same energy on every P and B.
  2. Standard 6 in fabric or metal-mesh pop filter, 2 in in front of the grille. The mouth stays where it was for the NONE take, so the filter sits between mouth and grille, about 1 in from the lips (use the 3 in end of the range for all three takes so the filter fits).
  3. Same taped gain as the LDC NONE take.
  4. Slate each take with the mic and barrier.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Check the filter is centred on the capsule, not on the mic body.

MPR-04a.3 — Large-diaphragm condenser — foam windscreen

1 file
Where it's used

Mic Principles › Plosives and Wind with the BARRIER tray on FOAM (readout: 50%). This is the large-diaphragm condenser version; the learner compares it with the other two barriers on the same mic.

What it teaches

Foam over the grille softens the blast (about 50% gets through in the app) but also takes a little off the top — the trade-off against a pop filter.

What to record

The plosive lines “Peter's best microphone sits six inches from the speaker — simple, steady, and clear.” followed by “Bob bought a big blue bass.”, spoken at 2–3 in on the LDC, foam.

How to make it
  1. DRY booth. Talker standing or seated, mouth 2–3 in from the grille, on-axis, at mouth height. One take contains both lines; same energy on every P and B.
  2. The manufacturer's foam windscreen for this LDC, fitted snugly.
  3. Same mouth position and taped gain as the LDC NONE take.
  4. Slate each take with the mic and barrier.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Use a clean, dry foam; a damp, used foam is duller than a new one.

MPR-04a.4 — Handheld dynamic — no protection

1 file
Where it's used

Mic Principles › Plosives and Wind with the BARRIER tray on NONE (readout: 100% of the blast reaches the capsule). This is the handheld dynamic version; the learner compares it with the other two barriers on the same mic.

What it teaches

A handheld dynamic has a ball grille and an internal pop pad, so it pops less than the LDC — but at 2–3 in P and B still thump. This is the live-stage reality for a singer who eats the mic.

What to record

The plosive lines “Peter's best microphone sits six inches from the speaker — simple, steady, and clear.” followed by “Bob bought a big blue bass.”, spoken at 2–3 in on the handheld dynamic, none.

How to make it
  1. DRY booth. Talker standing or seated, mouth 2–3 in from the grille, on-axis, at mouth height. One take contains both lines; same energy on every P and B.
  2. Handheld cardioid dynamic (SM58 class) on a stand, mouth 2–3 in from the grille ball.
  3. NO extra foam. Set the gain HERE so the worst pop peaks at −3 dBFS; tape it for the dynamic's other two takes.
  4. Slate each take with the mic and barrier.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record it last for the dynamic, after the pop-filter and foam takes.

MPR-04b.1 — Shotgun — bare (no wind protection)

1 file
Where it's used

Mic Principles › Plosives and Wind, the outdoor half, matching the NONE (bare mic) option. The learner hears wind with no voice, then the same voice through it, and compares the four states of the same shotgun.

What it teaches

Wind is moving air, not sound: on a bare mic it arrives as a loud, irregular low rumble that masks the voice. This is the problem the other three states solve.

What to record

Outdoors in a steady breeze: shotgun mic, bare; 20 s of wind alone, then a talker speaking S1 twice.

How to make it
  1. Open outdoor spot with a steady 10–20 km/h breeze (handheld anemometer; log the reading for every take). Avoid traffic.
  2. Shotgun on a stand at 1.5 m height, side-on to the wind. Talker 60 cm in front, on-axis.
  3. Each take: 20 s of wind alone (talker silent), then S1 twice. Deliver 4 s of wind plus both S1 lines; keep the full take.
  4. No protection at all. Set the gain HERE so wind peaks reach −3 dBFS; tape it for the other three states.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Its 20 s of wind-only is also the Noise Lab wind loop (NOI-01a) — mark it in your notes and keep the full take.
  • Shoot all four states back-to-back within a few minutes so the wind is comparable; repeat the cycle twice and keep the cycle with the steadiest readings.

LengthDelivered: 12 s (4 s wind, then S1 ×2); keep the full takes
LevelsWind peaks ≤ −3 dBFS on the BARE take
SetFIXED-GAIN (set on the bare take)

MPR-05a.1 — Handheld — grip shuffle

1 file
Where it's used

Mic Principles › Handling Noise and Isolation (“vibration travels through solids into the capsule”) and the Common Handheld Mistakes field guide. The learner hears this one noise under the voice and names its cause.

What it teaches

Re-gripping the handle sends rustle and low thumps straight into the capsule: the most common handheld noise, made by nervous presenters.

What to record

S1 spoken into a handheld cardioid dynamic while making one handling noise: grip shuffle.

How to make it
  1. Untreated medium room (or the booth if session 2 runs short). Talker standing, handheld cardioid dynamic (SM58 class) at 2–3 in. Fixed gain set on S1 for peaks at −6 dBFS.
  2. During S1, re-grip the handle twice: open the hand and close it again a little higher or lower.
  3. Slate the noise type before the take.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Use the same mic, cable and ring for all four takes; note them in the sidecar.
  • Record the four handling takes back-to-back with the same gain.

S1 spoken into a handheld cardioid dynamic while making one handling noise: finger tap.

  3. Slate the noise type before the take.

MPR-05b.1 — Desk knock — rigid clip

1 file
Where it's used

Mic Principles › Handling Noise and Isolation with the MOUNT tray on RIGID MOUNT (INTO MIC readout 90%). The learner flips between rigid and shock on the same desk knock and hears what the mount removes.

What it teaches

A knock on the desk travels up the desk stand and through a rigid clip into the mic body: it arrives as a heavy low thump under the voice (the app's 90% INTO MIC).

What to record

S1 at 15 cm on an LDC in a rigid clip, with a repeatable desk knock.

How to make it
  1. Podcast setup: LDC on a desk stand, talker speaking S1 at 15 cm.
  2. Knock: a tennis ball dropped from 30 cm (along a ruler) onto the desk 30 cm from the stand base, twice during S1 — identical impacts every take.
  3. Mount: the mic's rigid stand clip.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Tape the stand position and mic height so the mount swap changes nothing else.
  • Record rigid then shock straight away, same gain.
  • A tennis ball dropped along a ruler gives identical knocks every take.

Where it's used

Mic Principles › Handling Noise and Isolation with the MOUNT tray on SHOCK MOUNT (INTO MIC readout 15%). The learner flips between rigid and shock on the same desk knock and hears what the mount removes.

What it teaches

The same knock through a shock mount: the elastic suspension soaks up the vibration and only a little airborne sound is left (the app's 15%). The voice is unchanged.

What to record

S1 at 15 cm on an LDC in a shock mount, with a repeatable desk knock.

  1. Podcast setup: LDC on a desk stand, talker speaking S1 at 15 cm.

  3. Mount: the mic's own shock mount. Swap ONLY the mount: same mic, same position (taped), same gain.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Tape the stand position and mic height so the mount swap changes nothing else.
  • Record rigid then shock straight away, same gain.
  • A tennis ball dropped along a ruler gives identical knocks every take.

Footsteps on a wooden floor shake a floor stand: through a rigid clip each step becomes a low thud — how footsteps get into a recording on a quiet stage.

  • Record rigid then shock straight away, same gain.
  • Walk to a metronome so the steps land at the same moments in both takes.

MPR-06.1 — S1 spoken · LOW HANDLE grip

1 file
Where it's used

Mic Principles › How Your Hand Changes the Mic with POSITION on LOW HANDLE (PATTERN readout: INTACT). The learner moves the hand through the four grips and hears the rear guitar creep in as the pattern collapses; this is the spoken version.

What it teaches

Holding low on the handle leaves the grille and rear ports clear: the cardioid pattern is intact and the rear speaker stays rejected.

What to record

S1 spoken into a handheld cardioid dynamic at 2 in, held with the LOW HANDLE grip, with the quiet guitar loop playing from behind.

How to make it
  1. DRY booth. Performer standing, handheld cardioid dynamic 2 in from the lips, on-axis.
  2. Rear reference: a small speaker 1 m directly behind the mic (180°) playing a quiet, steady original guitar loop (FX-04 DI) at about 60 dBA at the mic, the same level for all eight takes.
  3. Gain: fixed, set on the CORRECT grip for peaks at −6 dBFS.
  4. Grip: LOW HANDLE — Hand at the bottom of the handle.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Photograph each grip for our art team; put the photos in the folder.
  • Feedback when cupped is NOT captured here; if wanted, it belongs in the SS-01 feedback session under SAFE-2.

P2 Session 3 · 5 recordings · 6 files

About this lab page

Mic Principles › Stereo Techniques. A TECHNIQUE tray switches XY, ORTF, AB and MID-SIDE; readouts say where the stereo comes from (LEVEL, LEVEL+TIME, TIME, MIX) and how safe it is in mono. Today it is silent.

Setup diagram

Reuse: FX-05 (Stereo Imaging lab), EAR-06, Meter phase/stereo, Binaural lab.   See also: EAR-06 FX-05

Recordings in this item: MPR-07.1 MPR-07.2 MPR-07.3 MPR-07.4 MPR-07.5

MPR-07.1 — XY — coincident cardioid SDCs at 90°

1 file
Where it's used

TECHNIQUE = XY (FROM: LEVEL; IN MONO: safe). The learner follows the walking talker across the image and sums to mono to hear nothing change.

What it teaches

A coincident pair images by level difference only: both capsules hear every sound at the same instant, so the mono sum loses nothing. The price is a narrower image than the spaced techniques.

What to record

The shared stereo performance, captured by an XY pair.

How to make it
  1. Live room, RT60 ≈ 0.8 s. All arrays 2 m from the performance line at 1.5 m height. Coincident pairs clustered on one stereo bar at the same point (XY above, M/S below); ORTF beside them; AB straddles the cluster. Before the take, clap at the exact centre and check every pair shows it centred — fix by moving mics, not by panning.
  2. XY: two matched cardioid SDCs, capsules stacked one above the other over one point, 90° between their axes, the pair aimed at the centre.
  3. Match the two gains on the guitar alone at centre so the image is balanced.
  4. Performance (20–30 s), one take for all arrays: fingerpicked guitar throughout at centre, 2 m away; shaker 2 m to the left; talker starts far left and walks slowly to far right speaking S1 twice.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Capture all four arrays plus the mono spot in ONE performance — the comparison is only fair if the performance is identical.
  • Use the same SDC model for XY and ORTF so only the geometry differs.

MPR-07.2 — ORTF — cardioid SDCs 17 cm apart at 110°

1 file
Where it's used

TECHNIQUE = ORTF (FROM: LEVEL+TIME; IN MONO: good). The learner compares its width and depth with XY and AB.

What it teaches

Near-coincident ORTF uses level AND a small time difference, like a pair of ears: wider and more natural than XY, while the mono sum costs width rather than tone.

What to record

The shared stereo performance, captured by an ORTF pair.

How to make it
  1. Live room, RT60 ≈ 0.8 s. All arrays 2 m from the performance line at 1.5 m height. Coincident pairs clustered on one stereo bar at the same point (XY above, M/S below); ORTF beside them; AB straddles the cluster. Before the take, clap at the exact centre and check every pair shows it centred — fix by moving mics, not by panning.
  2. ORTF: two matched cardioid SDCs, capsules 17 cm apart, 110° between their axes, pair aimed at the centre.
  3. Use an ORTF bar or measure capsule spacing and angle precisely.
  4. Performance (20–30 s), one take for all arrays: fingerpicked guitar throughout at centre, 2 m away; shaker 2 m to the left; talker starts far left and walks slowly to far right speaking S1 twice.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Measure 17 cm capsule-to-capsule, not body-to-body.

MPR-07.3 — AB — spaced omnis 60 cm apart

1 file
Where it's used

TECHNIQUE = AB (FROM: TIME; IN MONO: risky). The learner hears the widest image, then sums to mono and hears the low end thin or change.

What it teaches

A spaced pair images by arrival-time difference: the widest, most spacious picture, but when summed to mono one mic can be pushing while the other pulls, so parts of the spectrum cancel.

What to record

The shared stereo performance, captured by a spaced omni pair.

How to make it
  1. Live room, RT60 ≈ 0.8 s. All arrays 2 m from the performance line at 1.5 m height. Coincident pairs clustered on one stereo bar at the same point (XY above, M/S below); ORTF beside them; AB straddles the cluster. Before the take, clap at the exact centre and check every pair shows it centred — fix by moving mics, not by panning.
  2. AB: two matched omnis 60 cm apart, both facing forward, centred on the same point as the cluster.
  3. Performance (20–30 s), one take for all arrays: fingerpicked guitar throughout at centre, 2 m away; shaker 2 m to the left; talker starts far left and walks slowly to far right speaking S1 twice.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Keep the spacing exactly 60 cm and symmetrical about the centre line — measure from the centre clap point.

MPR-07.4 — Mid-Side — cardioid mid plus figure-8 side (raw and decoded)

2 files
Where it's used

TECHNIQUE = MID-SIDE (FROM: MIX; IN MONO: perfectly safe). The decoded file is what plays as stereo; the raw file lets the page show mid and side separately and set the width after the fact.

What it teaches

M/S builds stereo from a forward mic plus a sideways figure-8: L = M + S, R = M − S. Turning the side down narrows the image; at zero only the mid remains, so mono is always safe.

What to record

The shared stereo performance, captured by an M/S pair, delivered raw (two channels) and decoded to left/right.

How to make it
  1. Live room, RT60 ≈ 0.8 s. All arrays 2 m from the performance line at 1.5 m height. Coincident pairs clustered on one stereo bar at the same point (XY above, M/S below); ORTF beside them; AB straddles the cluster. Before the take, clap at the exact centre and check every pair shows it centred — fix by moving mics, not by panning.
  2. M/S: a cardioid facing forward (MID) and a figure-8 sideways (SIDE) with its positive lobe to the LEFT, capsules stacked.
  3. Performance (20–30 s), one take for all arrays: fingerpicked guitar throughout at centre, 2 m away; shaker 2 m to the left; talker starts far left and walks slowly to far right speaking S1 twice.
  4. Raw file: ch1 = Mid, ch2 = Side, no processing, not loudness-matched.
  5. Decoded file: L = M + S, R = M − S, side at unity; then loudness-match it with the other stereo files.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Confirm the figure-8's positive lobe faces LEFT by tapping that side before the take: the decoded tap must appear on the left.
  • The raw file stays raw; only the decoded file is matched.
Specs
ChannelsStereo (raw: ch1 = Mid, ch2 = Side)

LevelsPeaks ≤ −6 dBFS

MPR-07.5 — Mono spot — single cardioid on the centre line

1 file
Where it's used

The mono reference for the stereo comparisons, and the source used in Ear Training module 6: it is what the performance sounds like with no stereo information at all.

What it teaches

One mic gives no left/right information: the walker never moves, only gets nearer and further. Against it, every stereo array's width becomes obvious.

What to record

The shared stereo performance, captured by one cardioid on the centre line.

How to make it
  1. Live room, RT60 ≈ 0.8 s. All arrays 2 m from the performance line at 1.5 m height. Before the take, clap at the exact centre and check every pair shows it centred — fix by moving mics, not by panning.
  2. Mono spot: one cardioid 2 m away on the centre line, at the array height.
  3. Performance (20–30 s), one take for all arrays: fingerpicked guitar throughout at centre, 2 m away; shaker 2 m to the left; talker starts far left and walks slowly to far right speaking S1 twice.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Use a cardioid of the same family as the XY/ORTF SDCs so the tone matches the stereo files.

SPK-01.1 — Off-axis 0° at 4 m

1 file
Where it's used

Speaker Coverage lab and Wave lab Loudspeaker Coverage: the sound of a listener 0° off the speaker's axis at 4 m. The learner sets a dispersion pattern and aims the box, then hears what a seat at this angle gets.

What it teaches

On-axis reference at 4 m: full top end. Every angle is compared with it.

What to record

Pink noise then S1 through one 2-way PA speaker, measurement omni 4 m away at 0° off the speaker's axis.

How to make it
  1. Outdoors on a quiet day or in a large empty room. 2-way PA speaker on a stand, HF driver at 1.8 m; measurement omni at the same height.
  2. Programme per take: 5 s of pink noise, then the dry S1 (from SPC-04 clean) from a playback device. Speaker level about 85 dBA at 4 m on-axis; never change it.
  3. Preamp gain set ONCE at 1 m on-axis so the peaks reach −6 dBFS; tape it. Record the 1 m take first, then the others.
  4. Put the speaker on a turntable (or mark angles on the floor around its acoustic centre). The mic stays put at 4 m; rotate the SPEAKER to 0°.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Rotate the speaker, not the mic — the room (or ground) reflection pattern then stays the same.
  • Do all six angles in one run before moving the mic for the distance takes.
  • Log temperature and wind outdoors; note the speaker model and its published dispersion.

SPK-01.7 — On-axis at 1 m

1 file
Where it's used

Speaker Coverage lab and Wave lab Loudspeaker Coverage: an on-axis listener at 1 m. The learner compares distances along the axis (1, 2, 4, 8 m) to hear level fall without the tone changing.

What it teaches

Close to the box: the loudest take (gain set here). At 1 m the two drivers are not yet fully combined, so the tone can differ slightly from further back.

What to record

Pink noise then S1 through the same speaker, measurement omni on-axis at 1 m.

How to make it
  1. Outdoors on a quiet day or in a large empty room. 2-way PA speaker on a stand, HF driver at 1.8 m; measurement omni at the same height.
  2. Programme per take: 5 s of pink noise, then the dry S1 (from SPC-04 clean) from a playback device. Speaker level about 85 dBA at 4 m on-axis; never change it.
  3. Preamp gain set ONCE at 1 m on-axis so the peaks reach −6 dBFS; tape it. Record the 1 m take first, then the others.
  4. Speaker on-axis (0°). Move the MIC along the axis to 1 m. Do not change the speaker level or the preamp gain.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Measure from the speaker's front baffle to the mic capsule with a tape.
  • Keep the mic at 1.8 m height for every distance.

About this lab page

Mic Selection lab: the learner studies mic types (moving-coil dynamic, condensers, ribbon, lavalier, headworn, shotgun, boundary…) and response shapes (flat, presence rise, low roll-off, extended highs) and picks a mic for a job. Today it is visual only.

Safety: SAFE-3: never phantom on a passive ribbon. (Safety section)

Reuse: WAV-03 context (boundary mic).   See also: MPR-01 MSL-02

MSL-01.1 — S1 voice · Dynamic

2 files
Where it's used

Mic Selection lab: the learner studies dynamic mics and their response shape, then hears this one on speech against the other mics on the same performance. The MATCHED copy removes level so only tone is compared; the raw file keeps each mic's real output level.

What it teaches

A moving-coil dynamic on speech: a presence lift and a gentle top roll-off, so the voice is focused but less airy; it also hears less of the booth than the condensers. The broadcast and live-stage sound.

What to record

S1 spoken, through the dynamic, 8 in from the mouth.

How to make it
  1. Session 1, DRY booth.
  2. All eight mics (four core plus lav, headworn, shotgun, boundary) record the same S1 performance at once.
  3. This channel: Cardioid dynamic (SM58/SM7 class) in the cluster, capsule 8 in from the mouth.
  4. Core cluster: the four core capsules as close together as possible, all 8 in from the mouth, all aimed at the source.
  5. Fixed gain per mic, set on the loudest moment of this source; record once.
  6. MATCHED copy: loudness-match across the mics of this source within ±0.5 LU, after QC of the raw set.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • One performance, all mics together — the only fair comparison.

MSL-01.4 — S1 voice · Ribbon

2 files
Where it's used

Mic Selection lab: the learner studies ribbon mics and their response shape, then hears this one on speech against the other mics on the same performance. The MATCHED copy removes level so only tone is compared; the raw file keeps each mic's real output level.

What it teaches

A ribbon on speech: smooth, darker top and natural low mids; the figure-8 rear also hears the booth behind the talker. Kind to a harsh voice.

What to record

S1 spoken, through the ribbon, 8 in from the mouth.

How to make it
  1. Session 1, DRY booth.
  2. All eight mics (four core plus lav, headworn, shotgun, boundary) record the same S1 performance at once.
  3. This channel: Passive ribbon (figure-8) in the cluster, 8 in from the mouth, on its own preamp channel with phantom OFF.
  4. Core cluster: the four core capsules as close together as possible, all 8 in from the mouth, all aimed at the source.
  5. Fixed gain per mic, set on the loudest moment of this source; record once.
  6. Passive ribbons get NO phantom power — use a separate preamp channel with phantom OFF, or an inline switch. If you use an active ribbon, note it.
  7. MATCHED copy: loudness-match across the mics of this source within ±0.5 LU, after QC of the raw set.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • One performance, all mics together — the only fair comparison.

MSL-01.5 — S1 voice · Lavalier (chest)

2 files
Where it's used

Mic Selection lab: the learner studies lavalier mics and their response shape, then hears this one on speech against the other mics on the same performance. The MATCHED copy removes level so only tone is compared; the raw file keeps each mic's real output level.

What it teaches

A chest-worn lav: chesty, with less top end because the chin shadows the mouth's highs; it moves with the talker so the level stays steady. Clothing rustle is its typical problem.

What to record

S1 spoken, through the lavalier (chest).

How to make it
  1. Session 1, DRY booth.
  2. All eight mics (four core plus lav, headworn, shotgun, boundary) record the same S1 performance at once.
  3. This channel: Lavalier clipped on the sternum, about 20 cm from the mouth, cable taped so it cannot rub clothing.
  4. Specialist mic: keep it in its own working position (not in the core cluster); its position is part of its sound.
  5. Fixed gain per mic, set on the loudest moment of this source; record once.
  6. MATCHED copy: loudness-match across the mics of this source within ±0.5 LU, after QC of the raw set.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • One performance, all mics together — the only fair comparison.
  • Set the specialist mics' gains on a trial pass first: the lav and boundary sit much further from the mouth than the headworn.
