P3 Session 1 · 4 recordings · 4 files

About this lab page

Mic Selection lab › specification terms Sensitivity, Self-noise, Signal-to-noise ratio and Equivalent noise level. Today these are text and diagrams.

Reuse: Gain lab context, Digital noise floor.   See also: GAN-01

Recordings in this item: MSL-02.1 MSL-02.2 MSL-02.3 MSL-02.4

MSL-02.1 — Ticking clock — dynamic

1 file
Where it's used

Illustrates Sensitivity and Signal-to-noise ratio: the learner hears a quiet source on a low-sensitivity mic at high gain.

What it teaches

A dynamic's low sensitivity (a few mV/Pa) means a quiet source needs a lot of gain, so the preamp's hiss is heard behind the clock: low signal-to-noise.

What to record

A mechanical ticking clock at 30 cm on a dynamic mic, at the shared high gain.

How to make it
  1. DRY booth, quietest time of day (first thing; HVAC off, nobody else in the building).
  2. Same preamp model and the SAME high gain on both channels (e.g. +60 dB). Tape the knobs.
  3. Clock at 30 cm from the dynamic and the LDC, side by side; both channels record at once.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record this and MSL-02.2 in one pass — same ticks, same gain.
  • Note the mic's published sensitivity (mV/Pa) in the sidecar.

MSL-02.2 — Ticking clock — LDC

1 file
Where it's used

The comparison for MSL-02.1 on the Sensitivity term: the same clock at the same gain on a sensitive mic.

What it teaches

A condenser's higher sensitivity (often 15–30 mV/Pa) puts out a much bigger signal from the same clock, so at the same gain the ticks are far louder than the noise.

What to record

The same ticking clock at 30 cm on an LDC, at the same high gain.

How to make it
  1. DRY booth, quietest time of day (first thing; HVAC off, nobody else in the building).
  2. Same preamp model and the SAME high gain on both channels (e.g. +60 dB). Tape the knobs.
  3. Recorded in the same pass as MSL-02.1.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Note the LDC's published sensitivity and self-noise (dBA) in the sidecar.

MSL-02.3 — Self-noise — dynamic plus preamp

1 file
Where it's used

Illustrates Self-noise and Equivalent noise level: the floor under every recording with this mic.

What it teaches

A dynamic has no electronics, so its noise here is almost entirely the preamp's hiss at high gain — the noise floor is a property of the whole chain.

What to record

10 s of silence from the dynamic, isolated, at the shared high gain.

How to make it
  1. DRY booth, quietest time of day (first thing; HVAC off, nobody else in the building).
  2. Same preamp model and the SAME high gain on both channels (e.g. +60 dB). Tape the knobs.
  3. Put the dynamic inside an isolation box or under a heavy blanket in the booth; nothing playing; record 10 s.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record both self-noise takes straight after the clock, before anyone arrives.

MSL-02.4 — Self-noise — LDC

1 file
Where it's used

The LDC's floor for Self-noise: compared with MSL-02.3 and with the clock takes, it shows why a sensitive mic wins on quiet sources even though it makes its own noise.

What it teaches

A condenser's own electronics make some hiss (its published self-noise, e.g. 7–15 dBA), but because its output is much higher, its signal-to-noise on a quiet source is still far better.

What to record

10 s of silence from the LDC, isolated, at the same high gain.

How to make it
  1. DRY booth, quietest time of day (first thing; HVAC off, nobody else in the building).
  2. Same preamp model and the SAME high gain on both channels (e.g. +60 dB). Tape the knobs.
  3. Put the LDC inside the isolation box or under the blanket; phantom on; nothing playing; record 10 s.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Let the condenser warm up for a few minutes after phantom is applied before recording its noise.

About this lab page

Speech & Voice › Vowels & Formants: the learner picks A, E, I, O, U (AH, EH, EE, AW, OO) and sees tongue position plus a harmonic spectrum with the formant peaks (e.g. AH F1 730 Hz, F2 1090 Hz; EE F1 270 Hz, F2 2290 Hz). Today it is silent.

SPC-01.1 — Male · AH (father)

1 file
Where it's used

Speech and Voice › Vowels and Formants with AH selected: the tongue drawing and harmonic spectrum show F1 ≈ 730 Hz, F2 ≈ 1090 Hz (the app's teaching values). The learner plays the male vowel and compares it with the other four at the same pitch.

What it teaches

The most open vowel: jaw low, tongue low and back. F1 high and F2 low, close together. Same buzz (≈120 Hz) as the other male vowels — only the mouth shape, and so the formants, changed.

What to record

AH sustained for 3 s by the adult male voice at a steady monotone ≈120 Hz.

How to make it
  1. House speech setup: cardioid LDC at 8 in, pop filter, DRY booth.
  2. Reference drone in one headphone ear (≈ 123 Hz / B2) so all five vowels share one pitch.
  3. 3 s, steady level, no vibrato, no glide in or out: start and stop cleanly.
  4. Peaks ≈ −6 dBFS; loudness-match the five vowels and both voices to each other (±0.5 LU).
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record all five vowels of one voice in one take with 2 s gaps; cut afterwards.
  • Measure the pitch of the delivered file and write it in the sidecar.

P1 Session 1 · 8 recordings · 8 files

About this lab page

Speech & Voice › Voiced vs Unvoiced: pairs with the same mouth shape, folds off vs on (P/B, T/D, K/G, F/V, S/Z, SH/ZH, TH/TH). Today it is silent.

Reuse: De-Esser context.   See also: SPC-01 SPC-03

Recordings in this item: SPC-02.1 SPC-02.2 SPC-02.3 SPC-02.4 SPC-02.5 SPC-02.6 SPC-02.7 SPC-02.8

SPC-02.1 — ZZZ — voiced S

1 file
Where it's used

Speech and Voice › Voiced vs Unvoiced: one half of the ZZZ/SSS pair (same mouth shape, folds on). The learner plays the pair back to back and listens for the buzz.

What it teaches

The same hiss as SSS with the vocal folds buzzing underneath: a pitched hum below about 500 Hz plus the 4–10 kHz hiss.

What to record

ZZZ sustained for 3 s by the male voice. S/Z: tongue near the ridge, air over the teeth.

How to make it
  1. House speech setup: cardioid LDC at 8 in, pop filter, DRY booth. One male voice.
  2. Sustain 3 s, steady; keep exactly the same mouth shape as for SSS, switching only the voice on or off.
  3. Same gain for the whole voiced/unvoiced block.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record the pairs back-to-back in one take (SSS-ZZZ, FFF-VVV, SH-ZH) and cut afterwards.

About this lab page

Speech & Voice › Consonant Families: plosives, fricatives, affricates, nasals, liquids and glides, each with where its energy sits (e.g. S and Z peak around 4–10 kHz; nasals strong below 500 Hz). Today it is silent.

SPC-03.1 — Male · Plosives (stops)

1 file
Where it's used

Speech and Voice › Consonant Families with Plosives (stops) selected: the page shows how the family is made and where its energy sits. The learner hears each consonant of the family between two “ah” vowels, in the male voice.

What it teaches

Airflow is blocked completely, pressure builds, then bursts out: a short silence, then a click plus a low blast of air. The air blast is what pops a microphone.

What to record

Every plosive in an “a_a” frame, in order: aPa aBa aTa aDa aKa aGa; male voice.

How to make it
  1. House speech setup: cardioid LDC at 8 in, pop filter, DRY booth.
  2. Even level and pace: one frame per second with a 1 s gap; neutral stress on both syllables.
  3. Speak the frames in the order listed.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Print the frame list on a music stand at eye level so the talker does not look down off-axis.
  • Record all six families for one voice in one sitting, then switch voices.

Length≈ 8–14 s (per family)
LevelsPeaks ≈ −6 dBFS

SPC-04The eight speech problemsP1Session 1, 29 recordings · 9 files
P1 Session 1 Session 2 · 9 recordings · 9 files

About this lab page

Speech & Voice › Speech Problem Simulator: the learner picks Sibilance, Plosives, Mouth clicks, Nasality, Muffled, Off-axis, Excessive distance or Popping breath and sees the cause, what you hear, what you see and the fix. Today it is silent.

Reuse: SPC-05 (male clean), MTR-01 speech, SPK-01 playback programme, WAV-03 playback programme.   See also: MPR-01 MPR-02 MPR-04a SPC-05

Recordings in this item: SPC-04.1 SPC-04.2 SPC-04.3 SPC-04.4 SPC-04.5 SPC-04.6 SPC-04.7 SPC-04.8 SPC-04.9

SPC-04.1 — Clean reference — house speech setup

1 file
Where it's used

Speech and Voice › Speech Problem Simulator. Plays alongside every problem in the simulator as the A/B partner. The learner reads the cause, hears it against the clean reference, and picks the fix (placement first, processing second).

What it teaches

The reference every problem is judged against: the same voice, mic and distance with nothing wrong.

What to record

S1 by the house male voice.

How to make it
  1. House speech setup (LDC 8 in, pop filter, DRY). Set the gain here and tape it.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record the problems fresh on this setup rather than reusing MPR files: the A/B against the clean take only works with the same mic, voice and distance.
  • Do the takes in one block; slate each problem by name.

SPC-04.2 — Sibilance

1 file
Where it's used

Speech and Voice › Speech Problem Simulator. Problem: SIBILANCE (the orange hump above 4 kHz). The learner reads the cause, hears it against the clean reference, and picks the fix (placement first, processing second).

What it teaches

Intense hiss on S, Z and SH between about 4 and 10 kHz — piercing “ess” sounds that spit. Fix: angle the mic slightly off-axis, back off, then a de-esser.

What to record

S1 by the house male voice, recorded with this one problem.

How to make it
  1. Same voice, mic and taped gain as SPC-04.1 (clean).
  2. Remove the pop filter; talker at 3–4 in, on-axis, with naturally strong S sounds.
  3. If the take would exceed −3 dBFS at the clean gain, lower the gain and write the exact change in the sidecar.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Slate the problem by name.

Where it's used

The P and B air blast hits the capsule: low thumps and pops, one slow huge swing on the waveform. Fix: pop filter, mic slightly above or beside the mouth, high-pass.

  3. If the take would exceed −3 dBFS at the clean gain, lower the gain and write the exact change in the sidecar.

SPC-04.4 — Mouth clicks

1 file
Where it's used

Speech and Voice › Speech Problem Simulator. Problem: MOUTH CLICKS. The learner reads the cause, hears it against the clean reference, and picks the fix (placement first, processing second).

What it teaches

Tiny dry ticks from saliva as the tongue and lips separate — sharp spikes a close mic hears. Fix: water before the take, a little more distance, then a de-clicker.

What to record

S1 by the house male voice, recorded with this one problem.

How to make it
  1. Same voice, mic and taped gain as SPC-04.1 (clean).
  2. The talker skips water for a while beforehand; real clicks only — never added with fingers or by editing.
  3. If the take would exceed −3 dBFS at the clean gain, lower the gain and write the exact change in the sidecar.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Slate the problem by name.

SPC-04.5 — Nasality

1 file
Where it's used

Speech and Voice › Speech Problem Simulator. Problem: NASALITY. The learner reads the cause, hears it against the clean reference, and picks the fix (placement first, processing second).

What it teaches

Too much voice through the nose, or a mic aimed where the nasal path is loudest: a honky, pinched tone around 800 Hz–1.5 kHz. Fix: mic lower and closer to the mouth, then a narrow cut.

What to record

S1 by the house male voice, recorded with this one problem.

How to make it
  1. Same voice, mic and taped gain as SPC-04.1 (clean).
  2. The talker speaks with a deliberately nasal placement, and the mic is aimed at the nose from 4 in.
  3. If the take would exceed −3 dBFS at the clean gain, lower the gain and write the exact change in the sidecar.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Slate the problem by name.

SPC-04.6 — Muffled

1 file
Where it's used

Speech and Voice › Speech Problem Simulator. Problem: MUFFLED. The learner reads the cause, hears it against the clean reference, and picks the fix (placement first, processing second).

What it teaches

Something absorbs the highs: everything above about 1.5 kHz falls away and consonants blur. Fix: clear the path to the capsule first, presence lift only afterwards.

What to record

S1 by the house male voice, recorded with this one problem.

How to make it
  1. Same voice, mic and taped gain as SPC-04.1 (clean).
  2. Drape a folded thick cloth over the mic; change nothing else.
  3. If the take would exceed −3 dBFS at the clean gain, lower the gain and write the exact change in the sidecar.
Efficient method / pro tips

SPC-04.8 — Excessive distance — 48 in, live room

1 file
Where it's used

Speech and Voice › Speech Problem Simulator. Problem: EXCESSIVE DISTANCE. The learner reads the cause, hears it against the clean reference, and picks the fix (placement first, processing second).

Direct sound falls 6 dB per doubling while the room and noise floor do not: roomy, distant and noisy. Fix: halve the distance before touching the gain.

SPC-04.9 — Popping breath

1 file
Where it's used

Speech and Voice › Speech Problem Simulator. Problem: POPPING BREATH. The learner reads the cause, hears it against the clean reference, and picks the fix (placement first, processing second).

What it teaches

Fast inhales and exhales straight into the capsule: gasps and whooshes between phrases. Fix: turn the head to breathe, mic beside the airflow, windscreen; edit the rest.

What to record

S1 by the house male voice, recorded with this one problem.

How to make it
  1. Same voice, mic and taped gain as SPC-04.1 (clean).

About this lab page

The visual model is the phrase “This is a sentence with essess.” Today it is silent.

DES-01.1 — Male · “This is a sentence with essess.” (on-axis)

1 file
Where it's used

The De-Esser lab's model phrase, on What Sibilance Is, Threshold and Choosing the Frequency: the learner sets the threshold so only the S sounds trigger gain reduction, and tunes the detector to the male voice's S band.

What it teaches

A short phrase packed with S sounds isolates sibilance: typical male S energy around 5–6.5 kHz (a deep male nearer 4.5 kHz). The learner hears exactly which syllables a de-esser should touch and which it must leave alone.

What to record

“This is a sentence with essess.” spoken by the male voice, on-axis at 6 in.

How to make it
  1. DRY booth. A bright cardioid LDC at 6 in, on-axis at mouth height.
  2. NO fabric pop filter (it dulls the highs). A thin metal-mesh filter is acceptable; otherwise none, with the talker slightly softening plosives.
  3. Performers chosen for naturally strong S sounds (auditioned on this mic). Never exaggerate S sounds.
  4. Fixed gain per voice for peaks ≈ −6 dBFS on the loudest S. No de-esser, EQ or limiter anywhere in the chain.
  5. Speak the phrase naturally three times; deliver the best single phrase.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Audition several talkers' S sounds on this exact mic before booking: the lesson needs real, not dramatized, sibilance.
  • Check the S energy on an analyser while recording (typical male S energy around 5–6.5 kHz (a deep male nearer 4.5 kHz)).
Specs
ChannelsMono
LevelsPeaks ≈ −6 dBFS
SetMATCHED (±0.5 LU per voice across its four files)
RoomDRY

DES-01.2 — Male · S1 spoken

1 file
Where it's used

Normal speech for the De-Esser pages beyond the model phrase (e.g. Broadband vs Split-Band, Over-De-Essing): the learner hears what the settings do to an ordinary sentence with S, SH and plosives.

What it teaches

On running speech a de-esser must catch S sounds of different strengths; overdo it and the talker starts to lisp. This take shows where that line is for the male voice (typical male S energy around 5–6.5 kHz (a deep male nearer 4.5 kHz)), so the detector frequency set on the model phrase is tested on real speech.

DES-01.3 — Male · S2 sung (8 bars)

1 file
Where it's used

The sung example in the De-Esser lab: a vocal where sibilance changes with level, from the soft verse to the full chorus. The learner sets a de-esser that works on both halves.

What it teaches

Singing makes sibilance harder: louder chorus S sounds hit harder, and a threshold set for the verse over-de-esses the chorus (or the reverse).

What to record

The S2 melody (8 bars at 80 BPM, soft verse into full chorus) sung by the male voice, on-axis at 6 in.

How to make it
  1. DRY booth. A bright cardioid LDC at 6 in, on-axis at mouth height.
  2. NO fabric pop filter (it dulls the highs). A thin metal-mesh filter is acceptable; otherwise none, with the talker slightly softening plosives.
  3. Performers chosen for naturally strong S sounds (auditioned on this mic). Never exaggerate S sounds.
  4. Fixed gain per voice for peaks ≈ −6 dBFS on the loudest S. No de-esser, EQ or limiter anywhere in the chain.
  5. Singer performs the full 8 bars to a click or a guide in one headphone ear, soft verse (bars 1–4) into full chorus (bars 5–8).
Efficient method / pro tips

DES-01.4 — Male · essess phrase, mic 20° off-axis (placement fix)

1 file
Where it's used

The placement fix the De-Esser lab teaches before any processing: the learner A/Bs it with the on-axis phrase and hears how much a small turn of the mic already achieves.

What it teaches

Turning a bright condenser just 20° off the mouth softens the S sounds clearly, because the highs fall first off-axis, while the vowels stay nearly the same. Placement first, de-esser second. With the male voice (typical male S energy around 5–6.5 kHz (a deep male nearer 4.5 kHz)) the drop shows most in that band.

What to record

“This is a sentence with essess.” by the male voice, with the mic turned 20° horizontally away from the mouth.

How to make it
  1. DRY booth. A bright cardioid LDC at 6 in, on-axis at mouth height.
  2. NO fabric pop filter (it dulls the highs). A thin metal-mesh filter is acceptable; otherwise none, with the talker slightly softening plosives.
  3. Performers chosen for naturally strong S sounds (auditioned on this mic). Never exaggerate S sounds.
  4. Fixed gain per voice for peaks ≈ −6 dBFS on the loudest S. No de-esser, EQ or limiter anywhere in the chain.
  5. Same distance (6 in) and same gain as the on-axis phrase; turn the mic 20° horizontally away from the mouth (protractor on the stand or a marked floor line).
  6. The talker keeps facing where the mic was; only the mic turns.

Efficient method / pro tips

Recordings in this item: EQ-01a.1

EQ-01a.1 — Clean kick drum loop, 96 BPM

1 file
Where it's used

The source of the BOOMY KICK scenario. The app hides a +8 dB peak at 250 Hz (Q 1.4) on this loop and shows the story “the kick drum sounds thick and boomy — it swallows the bass line”; the learner sets one band, presses CHECK and hears whether the boom goes away. Because the app adds the boom, the recorded kick must start out clean, or a correct cut will leave it thin.

What it teaches

That “boomy” on a kick is a low-mid bump around 200–300 Hz, not the sub thump: a cut there restores punch while the 50–80 Hz body stays. Of the five loops, only the kick has its fundamental and its “box” this close together, so the learner learns to keep the cut narrow.

What to record

A clean, balanced kick drum alone: four on the floor with a few 8th-note pushes, steady velocity, to a 96 BPM click.

How to make it
  1. Tune the kick for a short, controlled note: a front head with a port or a felt strip against the batter head. It must NOT be boomy (the app adds the boom).
  2. Mic: a large-diaphragm dynamic (RE20 class) 15 cm outside the front head, on-axis toward the beater. This is a flatter capture than an inside “kick-in” mic, which is already scooped.
  3. No high-pass, EQ or compression anywhere. Set the preamp so the hardest hits peak around −6 dBFS.
  4. Play 12 bars to the click (three-pass method) and deliver the middle 4 bars, cut on the downbeat at a zero crossing: exactly 10.000 s (480,000 samples).
  5. Make the MATCHED copy with gain only: −20 dBFS RMS, peaks ≤ −3 dBFS (no EQ, no compression, no limiting).
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record it during the session-3 drum setup, straight after FX-01, so the kick is already tuned; only the outside mic is added.
  • Choke the cymbals and switch the snare wires off so no ring from the rest of the kit rides on the kick.
  • Check the take on an analyser before moving on: a smooth 150–400 Hz region means the app's +8 dB bump will be obvious.

EQ-01b.1 — Forte sung vocal, S2 chorus bars 5–7

1 file
Where it's used

The source of the HARSH VOCAL scenario: the app adds +7 dB at 3.2 kHz (Q 2) and tells the learner “the vocal gets painful when the singer pushes”. The learner finds and cuts the presence peak with one band. It must be a pushed, full voice, because harshness is a complaint about loud singing.

What it teaches

Harshness lives in the 2–5 kHz presence region, where the ear is most sensitive. Unlike the sibilant loop (EQ-01e), the problem here sits under the vowels, not on the S sounds, so the learner hears the difference between a broad presence cut and a narrow de-ess.

What to record

The S2 chorus (bars 5–7) sung at full, pushed volume, but with a balanced, unharsh tone.

How to make it
  1. House singing setup: LDC at 8 in, pop filter, DRY booth; no high-pass, EQ or compression.
  2. Warm the singer up on FX-03 first; then ask for the chorus at full voice without shouting or squeezing.
  3. Set gain on the loudest note so it peaks near −6 dBFS before matching.
  4. Sing to the house click and backing in headphones (keep headphone level low so nothing spills). Cut 3 bars at 80 BPM = 9.000 s on bar lines, with the loop point in a breath-free moment.
  5. Make the MATCHED copy with gain only: −20 dBFS RMS, peaks ≤ −3 dBFS (no EQ, no compression, no limiting).
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record it in the same block as FX-03 and DES-01 while the singers are warm; only the brief changes, not the setup.
  • Record both session singers and deliver the stronger one: one file only.
  • If the voice already sounds edgy at 2–5 kHz, move the mic slightly off-axis instead of using EQ.

EQ-01c.1 — Live handheld vocal on a riser, no high-pass

1 file
Where it's used

The source of the STAGE RUMBLE scenario: the app adds +9 dB at 60 Hz (Q 1) and tells the learner “something is rumbling under everything — you feel it more than hear it”. The learner should reach for a low cut. The real riser rumble in this file makes the app's boost sound like a real stage, not an added tone.

What it teaches

Sub-100 Hz rumble is the classic low-cut situation, and the reason high-pass filters are on every channel. It is the only loop in the set where real, mechanical low-frequency noise sits under the voice, so the learner hears that cutting below the voice costs nothing.

What to record

S2 bars 5–7 sung live into a handheld dynamic by a singer standing on a stage riser, with no high-pass filter anywhere, so the natural floor rumble is captured.

How to make it
  1. At the venue (session 5): singer on a stage riser, handheld SM58-class mic at 2–3 in.
  2. Preamp and console high-pass OFF; capture from the console's direct out at line level.
  3. Let normal stage activity happen: light footsteps, shifting weight, the riser flexing. No exaggerated stomping.
  4. Sing to the house click in an in-ear or a low wedge; cut 3 bars of S2 at 80 BPM = 9.000 s.
  5. Make the MATCHED copy with gain only: −20 dBFS RMS, peaks ≤ −3 dBFS (no EQ, no compression, no limiting).
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Check on an analyser that there is real energy below 100 Hz before you move on.
  • Record it in the venue's sound-check slot before SS-01 feedback work, while the stage is still quiet and wedges are low.

Where it's used

“Boxy/honky” points at the 400–1000 Hz low-mids. The guitar is the only loop whose problem sits in the middle of its own range, so the learner hears that a mid cut can open a sound up without making it quieter.

FX-01.1 — Stereo kit balance (faders and pans only)

1 file
Where it's used

The default programme in the Compression, Limiter and Distortion labs. The learner moves THRESHOLD, RATIO, ATTACK and RELEASE and watches gain reduction on a whole kit. It is a balance of FX-01.2–.7, so its dynamics must be untouched for the lesson to work.

What it teaches

How attack and release shape a whole kit: a slow attack lets the stick through, a fast one flattens it, a short release pumps, and heavy compression lifts ghost notes and room. Only the full mix shows the kit “breathing” as one.

What to record

A fader-and-pan balance of the seven FX-01 close and overhead tracks: no new performance.

How to make it
  1. Balance kick, snare, hi-hat, rack tom, floor tom and the overhead pair with faders and pans only: no EQ, no compression, no bus processing.
  2. Pan overheads hard L/R, toms to match their overhead image, kick and snare centre.
  3. Render the same 480,000-sample region as the tracks, peaks −6 dBFS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Bounce it the same day as the take while the kit image is fresh; note the fader and pan values in the sidecar.

FX-03.1 — Male lead vocal, S2 bars 3–8

1 file
Where it's used

The male vocal choice in the Reverb, Delay, Chorus and Compression labs; also a programme in the Gain Staging lab (GAN-01). The learner hears the effect sit behind a real voice and watches the compressor ride the jump from soft verse to loud chorus.

What it teaches

How reverb and delay sit behind a lower voice, where the tail can muddy the low mids, and how a compressor evens out a 6 dB+ jump in level. Compare with FX-03.2: the same effect settings land differently on a lower, fuller voice.

What to record

S2 bars 3–8 sung by the male session singer: soft verse into a full chorus.

How to make it
  1. House singing setup: LDC at 8 in, pop filter, DRY booth; no high-pass, EQ or compression.
  2. Sing S2 to the house click and backing in headphones (closed-back, low level): verse soft and close, chorus full voice. Keep the singer's distance constant; the level change must come from the voice.
  3. Fixed gain set on the loudest chorus note (peaks ≈ −6 dBFS); do not ride it.
  4. Deliver bars 3–8 = 18.000 s at 80 BPM, cut on bar lines.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record FX-03, DES-01 and EQ-01b in one block with the singers warmed up; only the brief changes.
  • Do the male take first, then swap singers without changing mic or gain structure (re-set gain only).

Where it's used

The guitar source for the Distortion lab and a clean source for Chorus, Flanger and Phaser. The app's distortion acts like an amp on this raw pickup signal, so the learner can drive it from clean to fuzz.

What it teaches

What a guitar pickup sounds like before any amp: thin, bright and very dynamic. It is the right input for distortion, and the learner hears how much of a “guitar sound” the amp adds (compare FX-04.2).

The DI output of the clean arpeggio take.

  1. Guitar → DI box → amp; clean A-minor arpeggios at 80 BPM to click. Print the DI and the amp mic at the same time from the same take (never re-amp later); cut 3 bars = 9.000 s on bar lines.

  3. Gain so the hardest pick peaks at −6 dBFS.

About this lab page

Meter lab: the learner switches teaching signals (speech, kick, snare, guitar, organ, music, plus generators) and watches peak, RMS, LUFS and VU readings. Today the signals are synthesized.

MTR-01.1 — Held drawbar organ chord, A minor, loop

1 file
Where it's used

The “organ” teaching signal in the Meter lab, alongside reused speech (SPC-04), kick (EQ-01a), snare (ENV-01), guitar (EQ-01d) and music (MST-01). The learner switches to it and watches peak, RMS, LUFS and VU settle on steady values.

What it teaches

A steady, sustained signal has a low crest factor: peak and RMS sit close together and every meter reads steadily. It is the opposite of the kick and snare, whose peaks run far above their average.

What to record

An A-minor chord held steady on a drawbar organ, no rotary speed.

How to make it
  1. Drawbar organ (or a clonewheel), stationary: rotary/Leslie OFF or stopped, vibrato and chorus off, percussion off. Note the drawbar setting.
  2. Capture DI from the organ's line out, or a mic on the speaker if there is no line out (note which).
  3. Hold the chord for 15 s with no expression-pedal movement; cut an 8 s loop. A ≤ 50 ms equal-power loop crossfade is allowed (an edit, not processing).
  4. Level: RMS ≈ −20 dBFS; raw, no processing.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Do ENV-02's organ swell on the same setup straight after.
  • Tape the expression pedal down so the level cannot drift.

Where it's used

What it teaches

A whistle is nearly a pure tone: one peak with almost no harmonics. When it glides, the learner links a moving spectral line to rising pitch.

What to record

A human whistle gliding slowly and evenly from about 1 kHz to about 3 kHz over 10 s.

  1. Booth (session 1), SDC at 30 cm, slightly off-axis to avoid breath noise.

GAN-01.1 — Real preamp noise at +60 dB, dynamic mic connected

1 file
Where it's used

The real noise floor the Gain Staging lab adds under its programme (FX-03 vocal, FX-04 guitar). When the learner sets gain too low early and makes it up later, this hiss rises with it.

What it teaches

That noise comes in at the stage where it happens: the preamp's own hiss, plus the mic's source resistance, is fixed once the gain is set. Later gain cannot remove it.

What to record

A preamp's noise with a dynamic mic connected, about +60 dB of gain, nothing playing, 10 s.

  1. Do it with MSL-02 at the quietest time in the booth; HVAC off.

  4. Record 10 s; no normalising, no processing.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record a second 10 s at +40 dB too if time allows (archive only).
  • Listen on headphones at a raised level before delivering: any hum tone means move the cable away from power.

WAV-01.2 — Clave hit, dry outdoors

1 file
Where it's used

A second dry impulse for the same Wave lab modules. Unlike the clap it has a pitch, so comb filtering and echoes act on a tonal hit.

What it teaches

A short, pitched impulse (a woody ring, typically around 2–2.5 kHz) shows comb notches and echo repeats as a change in tone, where the clap shows them as a change in texture.

What to record

One clave hit, outdoors.

How to make it
  1. Open grassy field at least 30 m from any building, wall or large tree; still air (no wind).
  2. Omni at 1 m from the source, 1.5 m high; wind cover on.
  3. Peaks ≤ −3 dBFS. Record two of each and keep the best.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Same spot and mic as WAV-01.1; just swap the source.

WAV-02.1 — Treated studio (≈ 0.3 s): omni impulse response, position 1

1 file
Where it's used

The mono impulse response of the treated studio at position 1. With a convolution step the app places any dry source (WAV-01, FX-03) in this room, and the Reverberation Laboratory draws it as direct → early → late → diffuse. Position 1 is the reference measurement for this space.

What it teaches

What the treated studio does to sound: a short, controlled decay of about 0.3 s with few distinct reflections. Measured on an omni, it is the room's neutral fingerprint, with no stereo cues.

What to record

Log-sweep impulse response of the treated studio, omni, position 1, deconvolved.

How to make it
  1. Source: a full-range powered loudspeaker (an omnidirectional dodecahedron is best if you have one) at 1.5 m height, at least 1 m from walls. Note its model.
  2. Mic: omni measurement mic, pointing at the source.
  3. Position 1: 4 m from the source (less only if the space is smaller — note it), 1.2 m high (seated ear height).
  4. Sweep: 10 s exponential (log) sine sweep, 20 Hz–20 kHz, followed by silence longer than the room's RT60. About 85 dBA at the mic. Record 2–3 sweeps.
  5. Deconvolve with the sweep's inverse filter (time-reversed sweep with matching amplitude correction). Keep the linear impulse and discard the harmonic-distortion images that land before it.
  6. Trim from just before the direct sound to RT60 × 1.5 or to where the tail meets the noise floor, whichever is longer; 10 ms fade at the end only. IR peak ≤ −3 dBFS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Do every capture in a space before moving on: sweeps at position 1 (omni + ORTF on the same stand, one pass), sweeps at position 2, then balloon, clap and S1 at position 1.
  • Capture omni and ORTF in the same sweep pass: one sweep feeds both files.
  • Use a log sweep and deconvolve: it rejects background noise and separates distortion far better than a balloon alone.
  • Record 30 s of room tone at every setup (archive; it tells us the noise floor). Keep the raw sweep recordings — we may ask for them.
  • Log temperature, humidity and room dimensions; photograph the space with the source and mic positions.

WAV-02.2 — Treated studio (≈ 0.3 s): ORTF impulse response, position 1

1 file
Where it's used

The stereo impulse response of the treated studio at position 1, for headphone and stereo playback in the Reverberation Laboratory and Ear Training M9 Reverb Recognition. It is the one the learner hears as “being in the room”.

What it teaches

The width and envelopment of the treated studio: a short, controlled decay of about 0.3 s with few distinct reflections, arriving from all around rather than from a point. Compared with the omni, the learner hears space as well as decay.

Log-sweep impulse response of the treated studio, ORTF pair, position 1, deconvolved.

  2. Mic: ORTF pair (17 cm spacing, 110°) on the same stand as the omni, aimed at the source.
  3. Position 1: 4 m from the source (less only if the space is smaller — note it), 1.2 m high (seated ear height).
  4. Sweep: 10 s exponential (log) sine sweep, 20 Hz–20 kHz, followed by silence longer than the room's RT60. About 85 dBA at the mic. Record 2–3 sweeps.
  5. Deconvolve with the sweep's inverse filter (time-reversed sweep with matching amplitude correction). Keep the linear impulse and discard the harmonic-distortion images that land before it.
  6. Trim from just before the direct sound to RT60 × 1.5 or to where the tail meets the noise floor, whichever is longer; 10 ms fade at the end only. IR peak ≤ −3 dBFS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Do every capture in a space before moving on: sweeps at position 1 (omni + ORTF on the same stand, one pass), sweeps at position 2, then balloon, clap and S1 at position 1.
  • Capture omni and ORTF in the same sweep pass: one sweep feeds both files.
  • Use a log sweep and deconvolve: it rejects background noise and separates distortion far better than a balloon alone.
  • Record 30 s of room tone at every setup (archive; it tells us the noise floor). Keep the raw sweep recordings — we may ask for them.
  • Log temperature, humidity and room dimensions; photograph the space with the source and mic positions.

WAV-02.3 — Treated studio (≈ 0.3 s): omni impulse response, position 2

1 file
Where it's used

The mono impulse response of the treated studio at position 2. With a convolution step the app places any dry source (WAV-01, FX-03) in this room, and the Reverberation Laboratory draws it as direct → early → late → diffuse. Position 2 lets the app show the same room from a second seat.

What it teaches

What the treated studio does to sound: a short, controlled decay of about 0.3 s with few distinct reflections. Against position 1 the late decay stays about the same while the early reflections and the direct-to-reverberant balance change: decay time belongs to the room, the early pattern to the seat.

Log-sweep impulse response of the treated studio, omni, position 2, deconvolved.

  2. Mic: omni measurement mic, pointing at the source.
  3. Position 2: at least 2 m from position 1 and not symmetrical with it, same height; log the distance to the source.
  4. Sweep: 10 s exponential (log) sine sweep, 20 Hz–20 kHz, followed by silence longer than the room's RT60. About 85 dBA at the mic. Record 2–3 sweeps.
  5. Deconvolve with the sweep's inverse filter (time-reversed sweep with matching amplitude correction). Keep the linear impulse and discard the harmonic-distortion images that land before it.
  6. Trim from just before the direct sound to RT60 × 1.5 or to where the tail meets the noise floor, whichever is longer; 10 ms fade at the end only. IR peak ≤ −3 dBFS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Do every capture in a space before moving on: sweeps at position 1 (omni + ORTF on the same stand, one pass), sweeps at position 2, then balloon, clap and S1 at position 1.
  • Capture omni and ORTF in the same sweep pass: one sweep feeds both files.
  • Use a log sweep and deconvolve: it rejects background noise and separates distortion far better than a balloon alone.
  • Record 30 s of room tone at every setup (archive; it tells us the noise floor). Keep the raw sweep recordings — we may ask for them.
  • Log temperature, humidity and room dimensions; photograph the space with the source and mic positions.

WAV-02.5 — Treated studio (≈ 0.3 s): balloon pop (ORTF, position 1)

1 file
Where it's used

A real impulse in the treated studio that plays back with no convolution step, and the cross-check of the sweep IRs. The learner can hear the room's decay on a sound they recognise.

What it teaches

The decay of the treated studio excited by a single acoustic bang: a short, controlled decay of about 0.3 s with few distinct reflections. Unlike the sweep IR it carries a little of the balloon's own colour, a lesson in why engineers prefer sweeps for measurement.

What to record

One balloon popped at the source position in the treated studio, captured by the ORTF pair at position 1.

How to make it
  1. Same rig as the position-1 IRs: ORTF pair at position 1, 1.2 m high.
  2. Inflate a standard party balloon to the same size each time (about 30 cm); pop it with a pin at the loudspeaker's position, 1.5 m high.
  3. Pop 2–3 and keep the cleanest; trim like an IR (RT60 × 1.5, 10 ms end fade).
  4. Turn the preamp down first: a balloon is far louder than the sweep; peak ≤ −3 dBFS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Pop the balloons straight after the position-1 sweeps without touching the stands.

  6. Trim from just before the direct sound to RT60 × 1.5 or to where the tail meets the noise floor, whichever is longer; 10 ms fade at the end only. IR peak ≤ −3 dBFS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Do every capture in a space before moving on: sweeps at position 1 (omni + ORTF on the same stand, one pass), sweeps at position 2, then balloon, clap and S1 at position 1.
  • Capture omni and ORTF in the same sweep pass: one sweep feeds both files.
  • Use a log sweep and deconvolve: it rejects background noise and separates distortion far better than a balloon alone.
  • Record 30 s of room tone at every setup (archive; it tells us the noise floor). Keep the raw sweep recordings — we may ask for them.
  • Log temperature, humidity and room dimensions; photograph the space with the source and mic positions.

WAV-02.26 — Gym or church (≈ 2 s): balloon pop (ORTF, position 1)

1 file
Where it's used

A real impulse in the gym or church that plays back with no convolution step, and the cross-check of the sweep IRs. The learner can hear the room's decay on a sound they recognise.

What it teaches

The decay of the gym or church excited by a single acoustic bang: a long, dense decay of about 2 s. Unlike the sweep IR it carries a little of the balloon's own colour, a lesson in why engineers prefer sweeps for measurement.

What to record

One balloon popped at the source position in the gym or church, captured by the ORTF pair at position 1.

How to make it
  1. Same rig as the position-1 IRs: ORTF pair at position 1, 1.2 m high.
  2. Inflate a standard party balloon to the same size each time (about 30 cm); pop it with a pin at the loudspeaker's position, 1.5 m high.
  3. Pop 2–3 and keep the cleanest; trim like an IR (RT60 × 1.5, 10 ms end fade).
  4. Turn the preamp down first: a balloon is far louder than the sweep; peak ≤ −3 dBFS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Pop the balloons straight after the position-1 sweeps without touching the stands.

A real impulse in the concrete stairwell that plays back with no convolution step, and the cross-check of the sweep IRs. The learner can hear the room's decay on a sound they recognise.

What it teaches

The decay of the concrete stairwell excited by a single acoustic bang: flutter echo: a rapid, buzzy repeating echo between parallel hard walls. Unlike the sweep IR it carries a little of the balloon's own colour, a lesson in why engineers prefer sweeps for measurement.

What to record

One balloon popped at the source position in the concrete stairwell, captured by the ORTF pair at position 1.

How to make it
  1. Same rig as the position-1 IRs: ORTF pair at position 1, 1.2 m high.
  2. Inflate a standard party balloon to the same size each time (about 30 cm); pop it with a pin at the loudspeaker's position, 1.5 m high.
  3. Pop 2–3 and keep the cleanest; trim like an IR (RT60 × 1.5, 10 ms end fade).
  4. Turn the preamp down first: a balloon is far louder than the sweep; peak ≤ −3 dBFS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Pop the balloons straight after the position-1 sweeps without touching the stands.

WAV-02.36 — Hall or large church (session 5 venue): omni impulse response, position 1

1 file
Where it's used

The mono impulse response of the hall or large church (session-5 venue, empty, HVAC off) at position 1. With a convolution step the app places any dry source (WAV-01, FX-03) in this room, and the Reverberation Laboratory draws it as direct → early → late → diffuse. Position 1 is the reference measurement for this space.

What it teaches

What the hall or large church (session-5 venue, empty, HVAC off) does to sound: a long, smooth, enveloping decay with a clear gap between the direct sound and the reverberant field. Measured on an omni, it is the room's neutral fingerprint, with no stereo cues.

What to record

Log-sweep impulse response of the hall or large church (session-5 venue, empty, HVAC off), omni, position 1, deconvolved.

How to make it
  1. Source: a full-range powered loudspeaker (an omnidirectional dodecahedron is best if you have one) at 1.5 m height, at least 1 m from walls. Note its model.
  2. Mic: omni measurement mic, pointing at the source.
  3. Position 1: 4 m from the source (less only if the space is smaller — note it), 1.2 m high (seated ear height).
  4. Sweep: 10 s exponential (log) sine sweep, 20 Hz–20 kHz, followed by silence longer than the room's RT60. About 85 dBA at the mic. Record 2–3 sweeps.
  5. Deconvolve with the sweep's inverse filter (time-reversed sweep with matching amplitude correction). Keep the linear impulse and discard the harmonic-distortion images that land before it.
  6. Trim from just before the direct sound to RT60 × 1.5 or to where the tail meets the noise floor, whichever is longer; 10 ms fade at the end only. IR peak ≤ −3 dBFS.
  7. The hall IRs are done at the session-5 venue (empty, HVAC off) with the same rig.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Do every capture in a space before moving on: sweeps at position 1 (omni + ORTF on the same stand, one pass), sweeps at position 2, then balloon, clap and S1 at position 1.
  • Capture omni and ORTF in the same sweep pass: one sweep feeds both files.
  • Use a log sweep and deconvolve: it rejects background noise and separates distortion far better than a balloon alone.
  • Record 30 s of room tone at every setup (archive; it tells us the noise floor). Keep the raw sweep recordings — we may ask for them.
  • Log temperature, humidity and room dimensions; photograph the space with the source and mic positions.

About this lab page

Wave lab Comb Filtering Laboratory (“one reflection plus the direct sound — move the microphone six inches”). Today it is drawn and synthesized.

Setup diagram

Reuse: Phase lab, Flanger, Mic Selection (boundary).   See also: MSL-01 FX-06

Recordings in this item: WAV-03.1 WAV-03.2 WAV-03.3 WAV-03.4 WAV-03.5 WAV-03.6 WAV-03.7 WAV-03.8 WAV-03.9 WAV-03.10

WAV-03.1 — Omni 2 in above the table: S1

1 file
Where it's used

The speech version of the same height in the Comb Filtering Laboratory: the learner hears what a mic 2 in above a table does to a voice, as at a podium, conference table or desk. At 2 in the table reflection arrives about 0.10 ms after the direct sound, so the first notch lands near 5,100 Hz with further notches every ≈ 10,200 Hz (approximate, for this geometry).

What it teaches

On a voice the comb is heard as a coloured, slightly “tubey” tone that changes with mic height. At 2 in the colour is subtle and only dulls the S sounds.

What to record

The dry S1 (SPC-04 clean) from the speaker, captured by the omni 2 in above the table.

How to make it
  1. Untreated room, a large hard table (wood or laminate) with nothing else on it.
  2. Small full-range speaker at seated mouth height (35 cm above the table), 1 m horizontally from the mic position, aimed at the mic.
  3. Same gain and same playback level for every take (FIXED-GAIN); peaks ≤ −6 dBFS.
  4. Omni on a stand pointing at the speaker, capsule exactly 2 in above the table top (measure to the capsule).
  5. Play the dry S1 (SPC-04 clean) for 6 s.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Using playback, not a live talker, makes every height identical except the reflection.
  • Batch it: at each height play S1 then pink noise, then raise the mic; finish with the boundary mic.

About this lab page

Wave lab Echo Laboratory: discrete echoes vs fused reflections and the ~50 ms threshold. Today the echo is synthesized.

Safety: Sweeps ≈ 85 dBA: protection for anyone nearby. (Safety section)

WAV-04.1 — Clap with wall echo, omni

1 file
Where it's used

The main example in the Echo Laboratory: the learner hears a clap, a gap, and a single echo, and checks the delay against the 2 × distance ÷ 343 m/s formula on the waveform.

What it teaches

Beyond about 50 ms a reflection stops fusing with the sound and is heard as a separate echo. In mono the echo's delay is easy to see and measure.

What to record

A hand clap facing the wall, with its real echo, on the omni.

How to make it
  1. Large flat wall (warehouse or school building) with open ground in front and no other reflectors near. Stand 15–25 m away (round trip ≈ 87–146 ms); measure and log the distance.
  2. Source and mics together, facing the wall: omni plus ORTF pair at 1.5 m height; the source (claps, the S1 playback speaker) 1 m in front of them.
  3. Early morning, no wind, no traffic.
  4. Clap 3–4 times, a few seconds apart; keep the cleanest; peaks ≤ −3 dBFS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Split from WAV-02 because the method is different: one wall, one echo, open air.
  • Do it the same morning as WAV-01, with the same person clapping, so the dry clap is a true comparison.

WAV-04.4 — Wall echo impulse response, omni (deconvolved sweep)

1 file
Where it's used

The measured version for the Echo Laboratory's waveform display: a direct spike and one echo spike, with the app able to convolve any dry source with it.

What it teaches

The impulse response of a single echo is just two spikes: the time between them is the delay and the height difference the echo's loss. It is the clearest picture of an echo there is.

What to record

A 10 s log sweep from the speaker toward the wall, captured on the omni and deconvolved as in WAV-02.

How to make it
  1. Large flat wall (warehouse or school building) with open ground in front and no other reflectors near. Stand 15–25 m away (round trip ≈ 87–146 ms); measure and log the distance.
  2. Source and mics together, facing the wall: omni plus ORTF pair at 1.5 m height; the source (claps, the S1 playback speaker) 1 m in front of them.
  3. Early morning, no wind, no traffic.
  4. Play a 10 s log sweep (20 Hz–20 kHz) at about 85 dBA; record 2–3.
  5. Deconvolve as in WAV-02; trim to 1 s from just before the direct sound.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Do the sweep last, after the claps and S1, so the louder sweep does not disturb the neighbours for longer than needed.

DIG-01Long quiet decays for bit depth and ditherP2Session 32 recordings · 2 files
P2 Session 3 · 2 recordings · 2 files

About this lab page

Digital Audio lab (bit depth, quantization, dither): the app will requantize a real decay to show quantization error growing as the level falls, and how dither helps. Today it uses generated tones.

Reuse: None.   See also: ENV-01

Recordings in this item: DIG-01.1 DIG-01.2

DIG-01.1 — Piano C4 decaying to silence

1 file
Where it's used

The main source of the bit-depth demonstration: the app requantizes this decay to 16, 12, 8 bits and fewer, and the learner hears the tail turn gritty as it falls, then hears dither turn the grit into smooth hiss.

What it teaches

Low bit depths fail at the quiet end: a long, smooth decay crosses every level from loud to silence, so the learner hears exactly where quantization distortion takes over.

What to record

One piano C4, sustain pedal down, left to decay 10–15 s to silence.

How to make it
  1. Quiet room, HVAC off; low-noise preamp; true 24-bit capture (no 16-bit stage anywhere). Aim for a noise floor ≤ −80 dBFS.
  2. Mic 30 cm above the hammers; peaks ≈ −6 dBFS.
  3. Play C4 once at mf, sustain pedal down; nobody moves until the note has gone into the noise floor. Record 3 and keep the cleanest.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • If session 7's freshly tuned piano is the studio piano, do the take there.

A second, musical source for the same requantize and dither comparison: quiet, detailed playing rather than a single decay.

  3. Ask for a gentle, pp–mp phrase ending on a ringing chord.

  • Record it straight after EQ-01d with the same guitar and mic, after moving to the quietest available room.

FND-01.1 — A3 (220 Hz): Piano

1 file
Where it's used

One of eight matched A3 notes in the Foundations timbre lesson and the Harmonics, Oscillator, Envelope and Meter labs. The learner plays them in turn, at the same pitch and loudness, and compares spectra: here a hammered, decaying tone whose upper partials run slightly sharp (inharmonicity).

What it teaches

Pitch is the same; timbre is what tells instruments apart. This note shows the only struck-and-decaying keyboard in the set: the harmonics fade at different rates.

What to record

A3 (220 Hz) held about 3 s at mf: Piano.

How to make it
  1. Close-miked (30–50 cm), DRY-ish room, mf, steady, no vibrato where the instrument allows; same mic for all eight.
  2. Mic 30–50 cm above the hammers; strike once at mf and hold the key.
  3. Tune to A = 440 Hz within ±3 cents; check every take with a tuner and log the measured cents.
  4. Keep the natural release; MATCHED to ±0.5 LU with the other seven (gain only).
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record all instruments in one block with the same mic and distance; book players back-to-back.

FND-01.3 — A3 (220 Hz): Flute — see note: concert flute cannot reach A3

1 file
Where it's used

One of eight matched A3 notes in the Foundations timbre lesson and the Harmonics, Oscillator, Envelope and Meter labs. The learner plays them in turn, at the same pitch and loudness, and compares spectra: here a breathy, nearly pure tone with few harmonics.

What it teaches

Pitch is the same; timbre is what tells instruments apart. This note shows the closest to a sine in the set, plus breath noise.

What to record

A3 (220 Hz) held about 3 s at mf: Flute — see note: concert flute cannot reach A3.

How to make it
  1. Close-miked (30–50 cm), DRY-ish room, mf, steady, no vibrato where the instrument allows; same mic for all eight.
  2. A concert C flute's lowest note is C4 (B3 with a B foot), so it cannot play A3. Use an alto flute in G (lowest G3) and note it — or tell production if no alto flute is available. Mic 30–40 cm, aimed between the embouchure and the first keys.

STH-01.1 — Steady hum at about 180 Hz, loop

1 file
Where it's used

One of the first real sounds a beginner meets in the Start Here lab: it plays on a loop while they look at the meter and the spectrum for the first time.

What it teaches

A hum is one steady pitch with a ladder of harmonics: a simple, stable picture on the spectrum, unlike the constantly changing shape of speech (STH-01.2).

What to record

A person humming with lips closed at a steady pitch (≈ F♯3, 185 Hz) and level for 8 s.

  1. House speech setup. Hum with lips closed, steady pitch (≈ F♯3, 185 Hz) and level for 8 s.
  2. Cut a 6 s loop; a ≤ 50 ms loop crossfade is allowed.
  3. Peaks ≈ −6 dBFS.

  • Use the session-1 male talker between other takes.

NOI-01a.1 — Staged café babble, unintelligible

1 file
Where it's used

The “speech babble” source in the Noise Lab, next to the generated colours. The learner hears and sees the noise that masks speech in restaurants and crowds.

What it teaches

Babble is the hardest noise for speech because it has the same spectrum and rhythm as speech; its energy sits in the 250 Hz–4 kHz speech band, unlike pink noise.

What to record

A staged café-style babble: 10–15 volunteers talking at once, with no intelligible words and no music.

How to make it
  1. STAGE it: 10–15 volunteers with signed releases talking at once in a medium room (counting, nonsense words, overlapping). No music.
  2. Do NOT record a real café: private speech and background music create privacy and copyright problems.
  3. Omni 2 m from the group.
  4. Cut a 15–20 s seamless loop (≤ 50 ms loop crossfade allowed). Match at −20 dBFS RMS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record 2–3 minutes so you can choose a steady 20 s.
  • Ask the group to keep talking through laughter; listen back for any single clear word and avoid it.

NOI-01a.3 — Road traffic

1 file
Where it's used

The “traffic” source in the Noise Lab: the outdoor noise that ruins location sound and drives isolation design.

What it teaches

Traffic is a slowly swelling low-frequency rumble with tyre hiss on top: most of its energy is below 250 Hz, which is why it passes through walls and windows.

What to record

A busy road from 10–20 m, with no horns or sirens.

How to make it
  1. Omni 1.5 m high, 10–20 m from a busy road; wind cover on.
  2. Choose a period of continuous flow; no horns or sirens in the delivered loop.
  3. Cut a 15–20 s seamless loop (≤ 50 ms loop crossfade allowed). Match at −20 dBFS RMS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record 2–3 minutes; the loop must not have one obvious passing vehicle at the cut.

NOI-01b.1 — 60 Hz hum from real gear

1 file
Where it's used

The “hum” source in the Noise Lab's electrical family, and the hum shape on the Meter lab's spectrum pages (MTR-02).

What it teaches

Mains hum is a smooth, low 60 Hz tone with a few soft harmonics: magnetic pickup from a transformer. The learner sees a single strong line at 60 Hz.

What to record

Hum induced into an unshielded input or a guitar pickup by a nearby power transformer.

How to make it
  1. Hold a guitar pickup (or an unshielded input lead) near a working power transformer (an amp's or a wall-wart's) and move it until the hum is steady. Never open equipment.
  2. Capture at line level into the interface: start at minimum gain and bring it up. Monitor on headphones at low level with a limiter on the monitor bus.
  3. Cut a 15–20 s loop at −20 dBFS RMS; peaks ≤ −3 dBFS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Line-capture electrical faults instead of acoustic ones: cleaner, safer, repeatable.
  • Do the hum, buzz and ground loop back-to-back on the same bench.

NOI-01b.2 — Single-coil guitar near a dimmer (SCR buzz)

1 file
Where it's used

The “buzz” source in the Noise Lab: the stage and studio noise a guitarist gets near a dimmed light.

What it teaches

Buzz runs at mains rate like hum but is harmonic-rich and edgy, with energy up past 3 kHz from the dimmer's sharp switching. The learner compares it with the smooth hum.

What to record

A single-coil guitar DI'd while placed near a dimmer-controlled light.

How to make it
  1. A plug-in or wall dimmer driving an incandescent lamp, set to about half. Never open the dimmer.
  2. Single-coil guitar (bridge or neck pickup) DI'd, held 0.5–1 m from the dimmer and lamp; strings muted.
  3. Capture at line level into the interface: start at minimum gain and bring it up. Monitor on headphones at low level with a limiter on the monitor bus.
  4. Cut a 15–20 s loop at −20 dBFS RMS; peaks ≤ −3 dBFS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Turn the guitar to find the loudest buzz; note the dimmer setting.

NOI-01b.3 — Ground loop

1 file
Where it's used

The “ground loop” source in the Noise Lab, and the real version of what Ear Training labels “(emulation)” today.

What it teaches

A ground loop's hum is mains frequency plus a strong set of harmonics (120/180 Hz audible), coarser than plain hum. It comes from current flowing in the cable shield between two earthed devices.

What to record

Hum from two mains-grounded devices joined by an unbalanced cable, each with its own earth.

How to make it
  1. Two mains-earthed devices on different outlets (different earth paths), joined by an unbalanced cable.
  2. NEVER lift a mains earth to create or cure the loop.
  3. Capture at line level into the interface: start at minimum gain and bring it up. Monitor on headphones at low level with a limiter on the monitor bus.
  4. Cut a 15–20 s loop at −20 dBFS RMS; peaks ≤ −3 dBFS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Plugging the two devices into outlets on different circuits usually makes the loop audible.

NOI-01b.4 — RF “dit-dit” from a 2G phone

1 file
Where it's used

The “RF” source in the Noise Lab and the real version of the Ear Training “(emulation)” label: the pulsed buzz a GSM phone puts into nearby audio gear.

What it teaches

RF interference is pulsed: a GSM phone's bursts rectified in an audio input give the rhythmic “dit-dit-dit” buzz, unlike the steady mains noises.

What to record

A 2G/GSM phone next to an unbalanced input or guitar amp input, during a call or registration.

How to make it
  1. 2G is largely shut down in the US: an older 2G phone on a network that still offers 2G may be needed. If not possible, say so — do not fake it.
  2. Phone 10–30 cm from an unbalanced input or guitar amp input; place a call to trigger the bursts.
  3. Capture at line level into the interface: start at minimum gain and bring it up. Monitor on headphones at low level with a limiter on the monitor bus.
  4. Cut a 15–20 s loop at −20 dBFS RMS; peaks ≤ −3 dBFS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • The bursts are strongest while the phone registers or rings; record a few minutes and choose the clearest 20 s.

NOI-01b.5 — Crackle from a dirty pot or bad connection

1 file
Where it's used

The “crackle” source in the Noise Lab: the sound of a worn control or a failing cable.

What it teaches

Crackle is a random rain of small impulses with no pitch at all, unlike hum and buzz. It points at a mechanical fault, not interference.

What to record

A dirty potentiometer or bad connection in a line signal path.

How to make it
  1. Turn a dirty pot slowly, or wiggle a worn cable, in a line signal path.
  2. Capture at line level into the interface: start at minimum gain and bring it up. Monitor on headphones at low level with a limiter on the monitor bus.
  3. Cut a 15–20 s loop at −20 dBFS RMS; peaks ≤ −3 dBFS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Old mixers and guitar amps have the best dirty pots; do not clean them first.

EAR-01.1 — Full mix (mono sum of MIX-01): excerpts A and B

2 files
Where it's used

Programme for Ear Training M2 EQ Recognition and M3 Band Identification: the learner hears A (dry) and B (one EQ move) on the full house song and names the frequency, direction, amount or band. Excerpts A and B are two interchangeable passages, so a round does not always repeat the same two seconds.

What it teaches

Hearing EQ changes on real music, not noise. On the full house song: every EQ move interacts with masking between instruments: the hardest and most realistic test.

What to record

No new recording: two 2.000 s loop-safe excerpts of the full house song, cut on the mix day.

How to make it
  1. Cut from the mono sum of the MIX-01 master stems (no processing).
  2. Choose passages with energy across 125 Hz–8 kHz (check on an analyser).
  3. 2.000 s will not land on a bar line at 80/96/100 BPM: put the loop point in a sustained moment and use a ≤ 20 ms loop crossfade.
  4. Mono. Match to −20 dBFS RMS, peaks ≤ −3 dBFS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Make all 12 excerpts in one sitting with one analyser setting.
  • Pick A and B from different bars so they are not near-duplicates.

About this lab page

Ear Training M10 Compression, M14 Clipping, M12 Polarity and M13 Comb Filtering: the app processes a drum loop (none/light/moderate/heavy compression, mild/moderate/severe clipping, summed copies). Today it is a rendered kick-and-snare pattern (spec: “V2: real drum loop”).

Reuse: SC-01.   See also: FX-01

Recordings in this item: EAR-02.1 EAR-02.2 EAR-02.3

EAR-02.1 — Straight groove, 100 BPM

1 file
Where it's used

The default loop for Ear Training M10 Compression, M14 Clipping, M12 Polarity and M13 Comb Filtering: the app applies none/light/moderate/heavy compression, mild/moderate/severe clipping, or sums a delayed or inverted copy, and the learner names what changed.

What it teaches

Recognising each process on a plain, even rock beat, where every hit is clear and evenly spaced: the baseline groove for hearing compression and clipping on transients.

What to record

Acoustic kit, 4 bars at 100 BPM: kick on 1, 3 and the and-of-3; snare on 2 and 4; hi-hat 8ths.

How to make it
  1. Same kit and mics as FX-01, re-clicked to 100 BPM. Toms and snare as for FX-01; no gates, no compression.
  2. Mono delivery: a fader-only mono balance of the close mics and overheads (no EQ, no compression).
  3. Three-pass method; cut exactly 4 bars = 9.600 s (460,800 samples); peak −3 dBFS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record the grooves at 96 AND 100 BPM in one sitting: the 96 is FX-01, the 100 is this item. Separate items, different lessons.
  • Play the three grooves back-to-back without touching the mics.

EAR-04.1 — Ground-loop hum, 60 Hz: two examples

2 files
Where it's used

A real example for the Ear Training M5 defect deck. Ground-loop hum: mains frequency plus strong harmonics, coarser than plain hum (the deck's “Ground loop (emulation)” answer, confusable with Hum). The two examples are interchangeable, so the learner does not memorise one file.

What it teaches

Naming “Ground loop” by ear from a real example, so the synthesized version (and any “(emulation)” label) can be replaced. A real ground loop has a harmonic signature a simple 60 Hz tone lacks; after this the learner can tell it from plain hum.

What to record

Ground-loop hum, 60 Hz, captured at line level: two typical examples, 4 s each.

How to make it
  1. Two grounded devices on an unbalanced link with different earth paths (outlets on different circuits).
  2. NEVER lift a mains earth.
  3. Defects are delivered SOLO (no programme), except clock-slip clicks and dropout, which need programme to be heard.
  4. Cut 4 s loops; peaks ≤ −3 dBFS; level-matched or quieter than programme.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Line-capture electrical faults instead of acoustic ones.
  • Record more than you need; choose the two most typical examples.

EAR-04.5 — Clock-slip clicks: two examples

2 files
Where it's used

A real example for the Ear Training M5 defect deck. Clock-slip clicks: the “Click” and “Digital glitch” family, from two digital devices that are not clocked together. The two examples are interchangeable, so the learner does not memorise one file.

What it teaches

Naming “Click / Digital glitch” by ear from a real example, so the synthesized version (and any “(emulation)” label) can be replaced. Regular clicks at a steady interval point at a clocking fault, not an edit.

What to record

Clock-slip clicks, captured at line level: two typical examples, 4 s each.

How to make it
  1. Two digital devices passing S/PDIF or AES with the receiver set to its own INTERNAL clock instead of syncing to the input, so samples slip at regular intervals.
  2. Programme: a steady tone or the EAR-03 bed through the link.
  3. Defects are delivered SOLO (no programme), except clock-slip clicks and dropout, which need programme to be heard.
  4. Cut 4 s loops; peaks ≤ −3 dBFS; level-matched or quieter than programme.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Line-capture electrical faults instead of acoustic ones.
  • Record more than you need; choose the two most typical examples.

EAR-05.1 — Plate reverb impulse response, wet only

1 file
Where it's used

The “plate” answer in Ear Training M9: the app convolves the test source with this IR so the plate choice is a real plate, not an emulation. Also used on the Mixing reverb pages.

What it teaches

A plate's sound: instant density and a bright sheen, with no room cues (no early reflections). In M9 it is the classic confusion with “hall”.

What to record

A deconvolved log-sweep impulse response of a real plate reverb, wet only.

How to make it
  1. Line in, line out: the sweep from the interface into the unit's input; record its output. No microphones, no SPL.
  2. Set the damper for a decay of about 1.6 s and note the setting.
  3. 10 s log sweep, deconvolve as in WAV-02; deliver wet only (no dry signal mixed in).
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Split from the WAV-02 spaces because it is a line capture through hardware, not an acoustic measurement.
  • Sweep and S1 on the same unit setting, back-to-back.

EAR-05.2 — Spring reverb impulse response, wet only

1 file
Where it's used

The “spring” answer in Ear Training M9, replacing the emulation.

What it teaches

A spring's dispersive, chirpy “boing”: high frequencies travel along the spring at a different speed from lows, which no room does.

What to record

A deconvolved log-sweep impulse response of a real spring reverb, wet only.

How to make it
  1. Line in, line out: the sweep from the interface into the unit's input; record its output. No microphones, no SPL.
  2. Use the unit as is; keep the sweep level moderate (springs misbehave when driven).
  3. 10 s log sweep, deconvolve as in WAV-02; wet only.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Do not knock the unit during the sweep: springs crash.

TUN-01Real piano octave stretchP3Session 77 recordings · 7 files

About this lab page

Tuning & Temperament chapters on harmonics and trade-offs: real pianos are tuned with stretched octaves because their strings are inharmonic. Today it is synthesized.

Reuse: DIG-01 context.   See also: TUN-02

Recordings in this item: TUN-01.1 TUN-01.2 TUN-01.3 TUN-01.4 TUN-01.5 TUN-01.6 TUN-01.7

TUN-01.1 — Single note A1 (55 Hz)

1 file
Where it's used

One of five single A's the Tuning & Temperament chapters on harmonics and trade-offs use to show a real stretch tuning. The learner compares its measured pitch and partials with equal temperament: on a stretched piano, A1 (55 Hz) is tuned slightly flat of equal temperament.

What it teaches

Real strings are inharmonic. This note shows the most inharmonic note in the set: the thick bass string's overtones run audibly sharp of whole-number multiples, and the fundamental is weak.

What to record

A1 (55 Hz) on a freshly, professionally stretch-tuned acoustic piano, held to full decay.

How to make it
  1. Book the tuner right before the session; ask for a normal concert stretch and record their stretch setting.
  2. Mic 30 cm above the hammers (mono), lid on full stick (note it).
  3. Play mf, hold the key down for 6 s or more; let low notes ring longer, never fade early. Peaks ≤ −6 dBFS.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record all seven files in one pass, low to high, straight after the tuner leaves.
  • Measure each note's pitch with a tuner app or analyser and log the cents from equal temperament.

Where it's used

What it teaches

A pure major third (5:4, ≈ 386 cents) sounds still and sweet, with no beating; players tune it about 14 cents narrower than the piano's.

What to record

SS-01.1 — ≈ 2.5 kHz, severity 1 — the ringy tail on speech

1 file
Where it's used

The first warning state on the Feedback control page: as the learner pushes the wedge SEND up, this is what speech turns into just before a ring takes hold. It is also the opening sound of the fault-bench symptom “a ring starts every time the singer's wedge comes up”, and the first wedge the learner hears in Soundcheck.

What it teaches

The early warning, in the presence band where vocal mics and wedges both peak: every word leaves a short metallic, hollow tail, but nothing sustains yet. The learner learns to act on THIS sound, not on the howl.

What to record

S1 speech into the vocal mic with the wedge send raised just to the point where each word leaves a ringing tail near 2.5 kHz; hold about 3 s, then pull the send back.

How to make it
  1. Venue PA session. One vocal dynamic on a stand 1 m in front of a wedge, aimed slightly off the wedge's null so it CAN ring. The talker speaks S1 continuously, 5–10 cm from the mic.
  2. Before anything else: a brick-wall limiter on the wedge amp, set well below the drivers' ratings; a second person whose ONLY job is the wedge mute; −25 dB plugs on everyone.
  3. Record the console channel's post-fader direct output (LINE) into the recorder. No room mic — or one at a safe level only.
  4. Steer the ring: a broad ≈ +6 dB boost at 2.5 kHz on the wedge's graphic EQ. Log it.
  5. Raise the send slowly while the talker speaks. Stop the moment the words grow a ringing tail. Hold ≈ 3 s, then pull the send back by 3 dB.
  6. Write down the send position where the tail started — SS-01.2 starts from it.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record SS-01.1 and SS-01.2 back to back without touching the mic, the EQ or the talker's position.
  • Slate “2.5 k, severity 1” before every take.
  • Take three or four passes and keep the one where the tail is clear but never sustains.

SS-01.2 — ≈ 2.5 kHz, severity 2 — the ring builds and is cut within 1 s

1 file
Where it's used

The danger state on the Feedback control page: the ring stops decaying and starts to grow. This exact file is also the Spectrogram tool's feedback demo (TL-02), where the ring shows as one bright horizontal line growing out of the speech.

What it teaches

What the moment of no return sounds like — a single tone that sustains and gets louder on its own — and that a cut within 1 s stops it before it becomes a howl. Severity 1 only rings; this one feeds itself.

What to record

Same set-up as SS-01.1, the send raised a little past the severity-1 mark until a 2.5 kHz tone starts to build; the second person mutes within 1 s.

How to make it
  1. Same rig and 2.5 kHz steering as SS-01.1; do not move anything.
  2. Start at the severity-1 send position, then raise it 1–2 dB at a time while the talker speaks.
  3. When a tone starts to sustain and climb, the mute person cuts the wedge within 1 s. Keep recording ≈ 1 s after the cut so the stop is in the file.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Rehearse the mute once at low level before the real take.
  • This is the TL-02 file: keep the speech before the build at least 2 s long so the spectrogram shows speech first, then the line.
  • Slate “2.5 k, severity 2”.

SS-01.3 — ≈ 250 Hz, severity 1 — a low ringy tail

Where it's used

The low-frequency version of the warning on the Feedback control page. The learner hears that rings are not always high and whistly; it is used so the notching exercise has a low ring to find as well as a high one.

What it teaches

A low ring sounds like a droning, boomy hang-over on the voice — easy to mistake for room boom. Hearing it next to SS-01.1 teaches that the ear has to search the whole spectrum, not just the top.

SS-01.7 — Ring-out sequence — each ring notched in turn until stable

1 file
Where it's used

The procedure the Feedback control page asks the learner to perform: raise the send, find the ring, notch it, raise again. Also the professional answer to the fault-bench ring symptom and the Soundcheck wedge-by-wedge step.

What it teaches

Ring-out as a method: each notch buys a few dB more gain before the next frequency rings. The learner hears 3 to 5 rings appear and disappear in turn until the mic is stable at a higher gain.

What to record

One continuous capture of a real ring-out on the flat wedge (no steering boosts): ring, notch, raise, next ring — 3 to 5 notches — until stable.

How to make it
  1. Same rig as SS-01.1 with ALL steering boosts removed (wedge EQ flat).
  2. Talker speaks S1 throughout. Raise the send until something rings (severity 1 is enough); identify it and pull that band on the wedge graphic EQ (or a parametric notch, about −6 dB, narrow).
  3. Raise the send again until the next ring; notch it. Repeat for 3 to 5 notches, until a further 2–3 dB of send no longer rings.
  4. Capture the whole sequence as one file. Log each ring frequency and the cut depth, with the time it happened in the file.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • The sequence can run longer than 10 s — deliver it whole; production will trim.
  • Do not call the frequencies aloud — the mic is live and on the line. Write them down.
  • Leave the final EQ in place for SS-01.8.

About this lab page

Sound Systems › troubleshooting fault bench: 22 faults, each a customer symptom in quotes; the learner walks the signal chain station by station to find it. Today the symptoms are text only.

Safety: SAFE-1 — line capture, gain at minimum first, limiter on the monitor bus. NEVER lift or defeat a mains safety earth; hum is made and fixed on the signal side only (isolation transformer or DI ground-lift). · Amplifier clipping: into a dummy load through a rated attenuator ONLY — never real speakers. The load's power rating must exceed the amp's output with margin. (Safety section)

SS-02E.1 — Amp clip — fault

1 file
Where it's used

Fault-bench card “It gets harsh and nasty as soon as the band gets loud.” The learner plays it before walking the chain; the answer is the amplifier, the first station with no headroom left.

What it teaches

Power-amp clipping on real programme: the loud passages turn gritty, flat and bright while the quiet ones stay clean — the sound of the last stage running out of headroom.

What to record

The house song through the bench rig with the amplifier driven into clipping on the loud passages, into the dummy loads; captured at the attenuator outputs.

How to make it
  1. Bench rig: console → stereo system processor → two-channel power amp → two dummy loads, each through a rated attenuator. Record the console main L/R (LINE) unless the step says otherwise. Programme: the house song (MIX-01 stems through the console, or MST-01.1) at a typical show level.
  2. For this pair, record the ATTENUATOR outputs (after the amp), not the console.
  3. Good partner first (SS-02E.2). Then raise the amp input (or processor output) until the clip lights flash on every loud beat. Nothing else changes.

About this lab page

SS-02A.1 — Buzzing driver — fault

1 file
Where it's used

Fault-bench card “The left top buzzes on every low note.” Every electrical station reads clean; the buzz moves with the cabinet — it is mechanical.

What it teaches

A damaged driver: a rattling, papery buzz that rides on the bass notes and sits on the LEFT side of the image, present even at moderate level.

What to record

The house song through the PA with an already-damaged driver fitted in a spare cabinet standing in as the left top; captured binaurally at FOH.

How to make it
  1. Venue PA, empty room. Binaural dummy head (or in-ear binaural mics on a person who stays still) at seated ear height; ORTF if neither is available. Programme: the house song at a moderate level (≈ 90 dBA max at FOH). Same position for the fault and its partner.
  2. Fit a driver that is ALREADY damaged (torn cone or rubbing voice coil) into a spare cabinet, placed as the left top. Never damage a driver on purpose.
  3. Good partner first (SS-02A.2) with a healthy cabinet in the same spot, then swap cabinets only.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Ask the venue or a repair shop for a known-bad driver in advance.
  • Record all four acoustic pairs in one FOH sitting, good first each time.

SS-02A.3 — L/R polarity at the centre seat — fault

1 file
Where it's used

Fault-bench card “Each side alone sounds full. Both together, the bass disappears in the middle.” One side is wired out of polarity; every electrical reading is normal. Also reused by Audio Scenarios (SCN-01) as a system fault.

What it teaches

Polarity cancellation: at the centre seat the low end thins out dramatically and the image goes vague and phasey, though each side alone is fine.

What to record

The house song with one side's polarity inverted, captured at the centre seat on the L/R axis.

How to make it
  1. Venue PA, empty room. Binaural dummy head (or in-ear binaural mics on a person who stays still) at seated ear height; ORTF if neither is available. Programme: the house song at a moderate level (≈ 90 dBA max at FOH). Same position for the fault and its partner.
  2. Seat: dead centre between the left and right mains (measure it).
  3. Good partner first (SS-02A.4), then invert polarity on ONE side at the system processor.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Measure the centre seat with a laser so both takes are truly centred.
  • Optional check: solo each side briefly to confirm each is full on its own (not delivered).

SS-02A.5 — Vocals in the subs — fault

1 file
Where it's used

Fault-bench cards “The vocal sounds boomy and thick — you can hear it coming from the subs” (an accidental vocal send to aux-fed subs) and the related wrong-crossover card.

What it teaches

A vocal in the subs: the voice gains a thick, chesty boom that seems to come from the floor and the sub positions instead of the tops.

What to record

The house song (vocal prominent) with the vocal sent to the aux-fed subs, captured at FOH.

How to make it
  1. Venue PA, empty room. Binaural dummy head (or in-ear binaural mics on a person who stays still) at seated ear height; ORTF if neither is available. Programme: the house song at a moderate level (≈ 90 dBA max at FOH). Same position for the fault and its partner.
  2. Aux-fed subs. Good partner first (SS-02A.6), then turn up the vocal's sub send (Aux 6) to unity — or, on a crossover-fed system, set the crossover far too high.
  3. Note in the sidecar which method you used.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Use a section of the song where the vocal is exposed.
