SS-02A.7 — Mis-set delay speaker — fault

1 file
Where it's used

Fault-bench card “Under the delay towers everything sounds smeared, like a slap echo.” The delay speaker arrives before the mains.

What it teaches

Wrong delay time: under the delay speaker each hit arrives twice — the delay first, the mains tens of milliseconds later — so the sound smears into a slap echo.

What to record

The house song captured under a delay/fill speaker 10–20 m back from the mains, with its delay set to 0 ms.

How to make it
  1. Venue PA, empty room. Binaural dummy head (or in-ear binaural mics on a person who stays still) at seated ear height; ORTF if neither is available. Programme: the house song at a moderate level (≈ 90 dBA max at FOH). Same position for the fault and its partner.
  2. Seat: under the delay or fill speaker, 10–20 m back from the mains. Log the distance.
  3. Good partner first (SS-02A.8) at the measured delay, then set the delay output to 0 ms.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Measure the correct delay (distance ÷ speed of sound for the day's temperature, plus a few ms) before the take; the app's Delay from Distance calculator gives the figure.

SS-03a.1 — Reference passage — male voice

1 file
Where it's used

The male reference voice on the Sound Systems speech pages (intelligibility, line check, coverage): the clean original the learner compares every PA version against. It is also the programme played through the PA for SS-03b.

What it teaches

What a clear, dry male voice sounds like at the source — every consonant crisp — so loss of clarity through a PA is heard as loss, not as the voice.

What to record

The 30 s reference passage read by a male talker in a dry booth.

How to make it
  1. DRY booth, LDC at 20 cm, pop filter.
  2. Natural, clear, even reading at about 150 words per minute of the 30 s phonetically balanced reference passage (House Scripts).
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Two complete takes; deliver the cleaner one.
  • Record SS-03a.1 and .2 in one booth sitting with identical mic placement and gain.

SS-03b.1 — Male passage · front seats

1 file
Where it's used

Sound Systems coverage and intelligibility pages: the learner hears the male voice as delivered to the front seats (close to the PA, where direct sound dominates) and compares it with the dry reference (SS-03a.1) and the other seats.

What it teaches

The best case: mostly direct sound, high clarity — the PA sounds close to the dry reference. Heard in the male voice.

What to record

SS-03a.1 (the male reference passage) played through the venue PA at a fixed level, captured at seated ear height in the front seats.

How to make it
  1. Play SS-03a.1 through the PA at a fixed level (≈ 75–80 dBA at FOH). Do NOT change the PA level between seats or voices.
  2. Binaural dummy head or ORTF at seated ear height in the front seats seat.
  3. Log the seat's distance from the PA and the measured dBA at the seat.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Do all four seats for the male voice, then all four for the female, without touching the PA.
  • Mark each seat with tape so both voices are captured at exactly the same spot.

AMP-01.1 — Clean, 10 dB below clipping

1 file
Where it's used

Amplifier Principles modules (bias, classes, Class D, real-world gain chain, diagnosis), which today are silent. This is the baseline the learner compares every other drive state against.

What it teaches

An amplifier working with 10 dB of headroom: it simply makes the programme louder and changes nothing else.

What to record

The house mix through the amp, set 10 dB below the point where the clip light first flickers.

How to make it
  1. Class AB power amp output → dummy load with a rated attenuator / line tap → interface. NO loudspeakers anywhere.
  2. Programme: the house mix (MST-01.1, the unmastered mix), summed to mono.
  3. Capture gain is set ONCE, on the hard-clip take (peaks ≤ −3 dBFS), and taped — the level differences between takes are real.
  4. Find the clip point (clip light flickers on peaks), then turn the amp input down 10 dB and record.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record the drive states in one pass from quietest to loudest (clean → just clipping → hard clip) without re-trimming the recorder.

AMP-01.3 — Hard clip, 6 dB over

1 file
Where it's used

Amplifier Principles modules (bias, classes, Class D, real-world gain chain, diagnosis), which today are silent. The damage state the diagnosis module warns about.

What it teaches

Hard clipping: flattened, high-frequency-rich waveforms that sound harsh and buzzy on everything loud — the sound that heats and burns tweeters.

What to record

The same programme with the amp driven 6 dB past the just-clipping point.

How to make it
  1. Class AB power amp output → dummy load with a rated attenuator / line tap → interface. NO loudspeakers anywhere.
  2. Programme: the house mix (MST-01.1, the unmastered mix), summed to mono.
  3. Capture gain is set ONCE, on the hard-clip take (peaks ≤ −3 dBFS), and taped — the level differences between takes are real.
  4. Raise the amp input 6 dB above the just-clipping setting. This is the take the capture gain is set on.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record the drive states in one pass from quietest to loudest (clean → just clipping → hard clip) without re-trimming the recorder.
  • Keep the take short — the dummy load heats up when driven hard.

Where it's used

Amplifier Principles modules (bias, classes, Class D, real-world gain chain, diagnosis), which today are silent. The real-world gain-chain module asks WHERE in the chain the clipping happens; this is one half of that pair.

Clipping upstream at the console is just as harsh as amp clipping. What differs is where you fix it. Heard as a pair with AMP-01.5 at matched loudness.

  4. Drive the console (or its output stage) into clipping by about the same amount as AMP-01.5; amp set well below its clip point.
  5. This pair is loudness-MATCHED, not fixed-gain: match it to AMP-01.5.

About this lab page

Cable lab and Connector Select (power connectors and analog lessons): the text explains that hum is solved on the signal side — isolation transformers, DI ground-lift — never by defeating the safety earth. Today silent.

Setup diagram

Safety: SAFE-1 — line capture, gain at minimum first, limiter on the monitor bus. NEVER lift or defeat a mains safety earth; hum is made and fixed on the signal side only (isolation transformer or DI ground-lift). (Safety section)

Reuse: None.   See also: NOI-01b EAR-04

Recordings in this item: CAB-01.1 CAB-01.2 CAB-01.3 CAB-01.4 CAB-01.5

CAB-01.1 — Ground-loop hum alone (60 Hz)

1 file
Where it's used

Cable lab and Connector Select (power connectors and analog lessons), which explain that hum is solved on the signal side — isolation transformers, DI ground-lift — never by defeating the safety earth. This is the bare symptom, heard first.

What it teaches

What a ground loop sounds like with nothing to hide it: a steady 60 Hz hum with buzzy harmonics above it.

What to record

The looped rig with no programme playing: hum only.

How to make it
  1. Two mains-earthed devices, each on a properly earthed outlet on DIFFERENT circuits (separate earth paths), joined by an unbalanced cable into the recorder's line input. That earth-path difference is the loop. NEVER lift or defeat a mains earth.
  2. Line capture. Gain at minimum first, then up. The same recorder gain for every CAB-01 file.
  3. No programme. Record 6 s of the hum.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record all four CAB-01 files without touching the recorder gain.
  • Same rig as SS-02E.7/.8 and the NOI-01b and EAR-04 ground-loop takes — record them as one block.

CAB-01.2 — Hum under music

1 file
Where it's used

Cable lab and Connector Select (power connectors and analog lessons), which explain that hum is solved on the signal side — isolation transformers, DI ground-lift — never by defeating the safety earth. Shows the hum the way an audience meets it.

What it teaches

Hum under programme: obvious in quiet passages and gaps, partly masked in loud ones — which is why it is easy to miss in a loud soundcheck.

What to record

The house mix played through the looped rig.

How to make it
  1. Two mains-earthed devices, each on a properly earthed outlet on DIFFERENT circuits (separate earth paths), joined by an unbalanced cable into the recorder's line input. That earth-path difference is the loop. NEVER lift or defeat a mains earth.
  2. Line capture. Gain at minimum first, then up. The same recorder gain for every CAB-01 file.
  3. Play the house mix (MST-01.1) at line level from the source device through the loop. Note the programme time you started at.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record CAB-01.3 and .4 from the SAME programme moment so the A/B is exact.

Cable lab and Connector Select (power connectors and analog lessons), which explain that hum is solved on the signal side — isolation transformers, DI ground-lift — never by defeating the safety earth. The first correct fix.

CAB-01.4 — Fixed with a DI ground-lift

1 file
Where it's used

Cable lab and Connector Select (power connectors and analog lessons), which explain that hum is solved on the signal side — isolation transformers, DI ground-lift — never by defeating the safety earth. The second correct fix — the one most engineers carry.

What it teaches

A DI box with its ground-lift switch engaged also cures the loop on the signal side. This is the safe ground-lift, unlike lifting a mains earth.

What to record

The same programme moment with the link replaced by a DI and its ground-lift switch engaged.

How to make it
  1. Two mains-earthed devices, each on a properly earthed outlet on DIFFERENT circuits (separate earth paths), joined by an unbalanced cable into the recorder's line input. That earth-path difference is the loop. NEVER lift or defeat a mains earth.
  2. Line capture. Gain at minimum first, then up. The same recorder gain for every CAB-01 file.
  3. Replace the unbalanced link with a DI box; engage its ground-lift switch. Same programme moment.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Check with the lift OFF first that the DI alone did not cure it (not delivered), then record with it ON.

CAB-01.5 — 50 Hz hum alone (OPTIONAL — abroad only)

0 files + 1 optional
Where it's used

Cable lab and Connector Select (power connectors and analog lessons), which explain that hum is solved on the signal side — isolation transformers, DI ground-lift — never by defeating the safety earth. An optional international version for learners on 50 Hz mains.

What it teaches

Ground-loop hum on 50 Hz mains is lower in pitch than the 60 Hz hum of CAB-01.1: the hum's pitch tells you the mains frequency.

What to record

Only if you are working on 50 Hz mains: the CAB-01.1 rig, hum alone.

How to make it
  1. Two mains-earthed devices, each on a properly earthed outlet on DIFFERENT circuits (separate earth paths), joined by an unbalanced cable into the recorder's line input. That earth-path difference is the loop. NEVER lift or defeat a mains earth.
  2. Line capture. Gain at minimum first, then up. The same recorder gain for every CAB-01 file.
  3. Only on a 50 Hz mains supply. No programme. Record 6 s. Never fake it by pitch-shifting.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Skip unless you are already working on 50 Hz mains.

CAB-02.1 — Unbalanced run beside a dimmer

1 file
Where it's used

Cable lab lessons on balanced lines and interference: the learner A/Bs the two cable types under the same interference. The dimmer case, unbalanced.

What it teaches

An unbalanced line picks up a dimmer's buzz — harsh and spiky, full of harmonics — right over the speech.

What to record

S1 at mic level down the 15 m unbalanced run, laid along a dimmer pack's load cable with the lamp dimmed to ≈ 50%.

How to make it
  1. Two 15 m runs laid side by side and left in place for all four takes: one unbalanced (TS), one balanced (XLR).
  2. Send a quiet signal (S1 speech at mic level) down each run. Identical receiver gain for all four takes.
  3. Lay both runs along the dimmer pack's load cable; dim the lamp to ≈ 50% (where dimmer buzz is usually worst).
  4. Record the unbalanced run.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Do not move the cables between takes — swap only the receiver input.
  • Record CAB-02.1 and .2 back to back.

1 file
Where it's used

Cable lab and Cable Install defect scenes, at the inspection point “crackle or dropout when the cable is flexed near the connector”. The crackle form of the fault.

What it teaches

Broken shield strands or a dirty contact crackle in time with the movement — the sound tells you to look at the connector end.

What to record

Programme through a genuinely faulty cable flexed near the connector once a second, crackling but not cutting out.

How to make it
  1. Programme: the house mix (MST-01.1) at line level through the cable under test into the recorder.
  2. Flex the cable near the connector in a steady rhythm, once a second, for the whole take.
  3. Use a genuinely faulty cable (broken shield strands or a dirty contact) that crackles but does not cut out.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Label the faulty cables and keep them out of service afterwards.

1 file
Where it's used

What it teaches

Why you mute before patching: a TS plug sliding into a live input shorts tip to sleeve on the way in and makes a loud pop and buzz.

What to record

A TS cable plugged into a live line input.

  1. Recorder only — NO loudspeakers anywhere in the path. Preamp/recorder at minimum gain, raised only as needed.

  3. Plug a TS cable (other end connected to a powered source with nothing playing) into a live line input at a normal speed.

PROD-01.3 — Remote guest double-ender (as received + 48/24 conversion)

2 files
Where it's used

Production / Post lab, Northgate episode 4 media stage: the learner ingests and verifies a media inventory of exactly these file names and must judge each row. The remote file is “sent by the guest”: 58 s at 44.1 kHz/16-bit. The learner must decide it is a FACT to handle (convert), not a fault.

What it teaches

A mixed sample rate is normal in remote work and is handled by a good sample-rate conversion; the low-quality laptop/phone sound is the real-world double-ender.

What to record

The remote guest recording themselves locally on their own laptop or phone mic at 44.1 kHz/16-bit, during the call — a real “double-ender”.

How to make it
  1. The remote guest joins over a real call AND records themselves locally on their laptop or phone mic at 44.1 kHz/16-bit — real low quality.
  2. They start a little late, so their file is ≈ 58 s.
  3. As authored: deliver their file exactly as received (44.1/16, 58 s).
  4. Clean: sample-rate convert to 48 kHz/24-bit with a high-quality converter — the only conversion allowed in this brief.
Efficient method / pro tips

A badly made edit clicks: cutting off a zero crossing with no fade creates a step in the waveform. It is repaired with a short crossfade.

An edit of host speech: a cut placed NOT on a zero crossing, with no fade.

  1. In your editor, take a host line from PROD-01.1, cut it at a point that is NOT a zero crossing, and join it with no fade so it clicks.

RD-01One small room before and after acoustic treatmentP2Session 612 recordings · 12 files

About this lab page

Room Design lab: Explore placement (modal pressure and reflections update as you move speakers and listener) and Add treatment (absorbers at reflection points, bass traps, a cloud, diffusers, a rug — compare with and without). Today the comparison is visual only.

Setup diagram

Safety: Sweeps ≈ 85 dBA: hearing protection. (Safety section)

Reuse: —   See also: WAV-02 TL-01

Recordings in this item: RD-01.1 RD-01.2 RD-01.3 RD-01.4 RD-01.5 RD-01.6 RD-01.7 RD-01.8 RD-01.9 RD-01.10 RD-01.11 RD-01.12

RD-01.1 — Before treatment · Clap at the good seat

1 file
Where it's used

Room Design lab, Add treatment: the learner hears the room's decay and early reflections on a clap in the bare room, and compares it with the treated version.

What it teaches

The bare room rings: a long, uneven decay with hard early reflections.

What to record

A single hand clap from the speaker position, heard at the good seat. (untreated room).

How to make it
  1. A small, bare room (bedroom/office size) with parallel hard walls and a pair of studio monitors.
  2. Binaural dummy head (or in-ear binaural mics on a person who stays still) at seated ear height. Same recorder gain for the untreated and treated passes.
  3. Good seat: the planned listening position (≈ 38% of room length). Boom seat: play a slow sine sweep 30–200 Hz and walk the room with an SPL meter; the seat with the largest bass peak.
  4. Treated pass: broadband absorbers at the first-reflection points, corner bass traps, a ceiling cloud and a rug (portable panels/gobos are fine).
  5. UNTREATED pass (first). Clap once, firmly, at the left-monitor position; let it ring out fully.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Mark every position with tape so the treated pass matches exactly.
  • Record all six untreated takes in one pass, install treatment, then the six treated takes in the same order.
Specs
ChannelsStereo (binaural)
Length6 s (IR as needed)
LevelsPeaks ≤ −3 dBFS

RD-01.2 — Before treatment · Speech (SS-03a) at the good seat

1 file
Where it's used

Room Design lab, Add treatment: the learner hears how the room affects speech clarity in the bare room, and compares it with the treated version.

What it teaches

In the bare room the speech blurs — reflections smear the consonants.

What to record

SS-03a.1 speech played through the monitors, heard at the good seat. (untreated room).

How to make it
  1. A small, bare room (bedroom/office size) with parallel hard walls and a pair of studio monitors.
  2. Binaural dummy head (or in-ear binaural mics on a person who stays still) at seated ear height. Same recorder gain for the untreated and treated passes.
  3. Good seat: the planned listening position (≈ 38% of room length). Boom seat: play a slow sine sweep 30–200 Hz and walk the room with an SPL meter; the seat with the largest bass peak.
  4. Treated pass: broadband absorbers at the first-reflection points, corner bass traps, a ceiling cloud and a rug (portable panels/gobos are fine).
  5. UNTREATED pass (first). Play SS-03a.1 (male reference passage) through the monitors at a natural speech level; capture a 6 s excerpt.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Mark every position with tape so the treated pass matches exactly.
  • Record all six untreated takes in one pass, install treatment, then the six treated takes in the same order.

TL-01.1 — Balloon pop, HVAC off (clean decay)

1 file
Where it's used

Audio Tools › RT60 Reverb Time: the tool records a clap or click, plots the decay, fits a line, and reports RT60, EDT, T20, T30, R² and the clean decay range. The good measurement the other two are compared with.

What it teaches

A strong impulse in a quiet room gives 30–40 dB or more of clean decay, so T30 is trustworthy and R² is high.

What to record

A balloon pop with the HVAC switched off.

How to make it
  1. Session-2 room with HVAC. Omni measurement mic at 1.2 m, 3–4 m from the source. Same position and recorder gain for all three.
  2. Include 0.5 s of noise floor before the impulse (the tool needs it), then let the decay run fully into the noise floor.
  3. HVAC OFF; wait a minute for the air to settle. Pop one balloon at the source position.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Do all three takes in one sitting; only the HVAC and the source change.
  • Bring spare balloons of the same size.

TL-01.2 — Balloon pop, HVAC on (decay stops ≈ −38 dB)

1 file
Where it's used

Audio Tools › RT60 Reverb Time: the tool records a clap or click, plots the decay, fits a line, and reports RT60, EDT, T20, T30, R² and the clean decay range. Shows the noise floor cutting the measurement short.

What it teaches

With the HVAC running, the same strong impulse decays only to about −38 dB before it disappears into the noise — enough for T20, marginal for T30.

What to record

The same balloon pop with the HVAC on.

How to make it
  1. Session-2 room with HVAC. Omni measurement mic at 1.2 m, 3–4 m from the source. Same position and recorder gain for all three.
  2. Include 0.5 s of noise floor before the impulse (the tool needs it), then let the decay run fully into the noise floor.
  3. HVAC ON. Same balloon size and position as TL-01.1.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record straight after TL-01.1.

TL-01.3 — Weak hand clap, HVAC on

1 file
Where it's used

What it teaches

A weak clap in a noisy room gives too little clean decay: the tool still prints a number, but it isn't real.

  3. HVAC ON. A soft, ordinary hand clap at the source position.

  • Clap softly on purpose; this is the bad example.

TL-04.1 — Tuning fork A4 (440 Hz)

1 file
Where it's used

Audio Tools › tuner and frequency counter demos: the steady reference the tuner locks onto.

What it teaches

A tuning fork holds one pure, steady pitch: the tuner needle sits still on A4 at 440 Hz.

What to record

A struck A4 (440 Hz) tuning fork ringing for 6 s.

  1. Booth, SDC at 10 cm.

FM-01.1 — Struck bell

1 file
Where it's used

FM Synthesis lab: the learner builds an FM bell and can compare it with this real one.

What it teaches

A real bell is inharmonic: its partials are not whole-number multiples, which is exactly what FM's non-integer ratios imitate — and its long, beating decay is what the FM envelope has to copy.

What to record

One struck handbell or tubular bell, full decay.

How to make it
  1. Mic at 50 cm, quiet room.
  2. One strike, mf; let it decay fully into the noise floor.
Efficient method / pro tips
  • Record both FM-01 sources in the same session 3 slot.

E · Recording session plan

Seven sessions. Within each, the shot list groups everything that shares a mic and setup, records the quietest captures first and the loudest or riskiest last, and names the items covered. Each session has a floor plan, an input list, the shot list and a run-order bar.

Gear across the sessions

Time1.5 days (one long day is possible if the podcast cast is booked for the afternoon)

PeopleAdult male voice talent (a LOW voice suits MPR-03); adult female voice talent; a male and a female singer with naturally strong S sounds (can be the same talents); Northgate cast: host, studio guest, remote guest (at home on a call); a hummer/whistler (any of the above). Child voice: skip (optional only with guardian consent).
GearMulti-pattern LDC (C414 class); bright cardioid LDC; second LDC; SDC; cardioid dynamics ×3 (SM58 class); true pressure omni; passive ribbon (separate preamp, phantom OFF); lavalier; headworn; shotgun on a boom; boundary mic; fixed reference cardioid; pop filters (fabric and metal mesh); foam windscreens for each mic; floor protractor, plumb line, headrest marker; small full-range rear speaker (for MPR-06); mechanical ticking clock; isolation box/heavy blanket; tuner drone source; tuning fork A4 with resonance box; finger-snap performer; laptop/phone for the remote guest; tape and marker for gain knobs.

F · Safety

Hard rules — no exceptions

  • NEVER defeat a mains safety earth. No lifted ground pins, no “cheater” adapters. Ground loops are made and fixed on the SIGNAL side only (DI ground-lift, isolation transformer).
  • NEVER drive real loudspeakers into clipping. Amplifier clipping goes into a dummy load through a rated attenuator only.
  • NO phantom power on ribbon mics (passive ribbons) or on unbalanced gear.
  • Feedback is cut within 1 s, with a second person whose only job is the mute.
  • Hearing protection for everyone during feedback work, sweeps, balloon pops and any loud session (−25 dB plugs for feedback).
  • Every clip delivered to learners peaks ≤ −3 dBFS — except the mastered references (MIX-03 at −1 dBTP, MST-01 b at −0.1 dBTP, MST-02 as written), where the level is the lesson; production sets their playback level in the app. Do not lower them. Fault clips are level-matched with, or quieter than, the programme.

SAFE-1 · Hum, buzz, RF, crackle, clocking, dropouts

  • Capture at line level straight into the interface.
  • Monitor on headphones at low level with a limiter on the monitor bus.
  • Start every capture with the gain at minimum and bring it up.
  • Never lift a mains safety earth. Use a DI or isolation-transformer ground-lift only.

SAFE-2 · Feedback

  • Record from the console's direct or post-fader output, not acoustically.
  • A brick-wall limiter on the wedge amp, set well below the drivers' ratings.
  • Cut any ring within 1 s, with a second person on the mute.
  • Everyone wears −25 dB plugs.
  • Never chase a full howl; the onset is the lesson.
  • Log the SPL ceiling (≤ 95 dBA peak at 1 m).

SAFE-3 · Phantom-power thumps and hot-plug pops

  • No loudspeakers in the path: recorder only, preamp at minimum gain.
  • Use a robust condenser mic.
  • Never apply phantom power to ribbon mics or unbalanced gear.
  • Let the phantom power drain between takes.

Amplifier clipping

  • Dummy load and a rated attenuator only. Never real speakers. Check the load's power rating exceeds the amp's output with margin.

Room sweeps and impulse responses

  • Sweeps at about 85 dBA at the mic; everyone in the room wears hearing protection. Balloon pops are loud at close range — protect ears.
  • Warn building occupants before sweeps.

Venue programme levels

  • Acoustic fault and monitor captures at moderate level (≤ ≈ 90–95 dBA). The buzzing-driver fault uses a driver that is ALREADY damaged — never damage one on purpose.

How this brief splits the source list's merged entries
